articles.title: Trump threw 'tantrum' during Kennedy Center meeting, congresswoman says
articles.summary: President Donald Trump threw a "tantrum" when he learned a federal judge had again blocked his name from the Kennedy Center, a board member recounts.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump threw a "tantrum" during a Kennedy Center board meeting when he learned that a federal judge blocked his administration's latest effort to put his name on the institution's building, according to a Democratic congresswoman who serves on the board.

Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, the lead plaintiff who the judge sided with in his ruling, recounted the heated Sept. 15 meeting in an appearance on MS NOW . She said the meeting, conducted on Zoom, opened with an update: in the case of Beaty v. Trump, "Beatty had been victorious."

"And he went into a tantrum," Beatty said. "I mean, let me just make it simple. It was the most unprofessional thing that I've ever witnessed or been a part of. He went into name-calling, everything from trying to say that I was an obstructionist, I was dumb. He said, 'I think you're incompetent.' And I said, 'I know you're incompetent.'"

Trump was in attendance as the board's chairman after appointing himself to the role weeks into his second White House term.

Shortly before the board met, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center's plan to add an inscription below the building's sign to honor Trump's financial contributions violates federal law and the judge's previous ruling in May ordering the Kennedy Center to remove Trump's name from the center's title and signage.

As the president aired his frustrations to her, Beatty said she asked the president, "'Are we really going to do this? This is really unprofessional.' But I was not going to let him call me awful things. And he said he was going to hold me responsible if something fell out of the ceiling (of the Kennedy Center) and killed someone."

Trump threw a "tantrum" during a Kennedy Center board meeting when he learned that a federal judge blocked his administration's latest effort to put his name on the institution's building, according to a Democratic congresswoman who serves on the board. Shortly before the board met, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center's plan to add an inscription below the building's sign to honor Trump's financial contributions violates federal law and the judge's previous ruling in May ordering the Kennedy Center to remove Trump's name from the center's title and signage.

"And I told him, I said, 'You're already killing people. We're at war. We also have people who are starving,'" the congresswoman added.

The board, composed mostly of Trump loyalists handpicked by the president, voted at the meeting to close the bulk of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts immediately for renovations pushed by Trump. Kennedy Center officials aligned with Trump say the building has fallen into disrepair, posing safety hazards to people attending shows. Officials have also warned about severe financial troubles and potential bankruptcy unless Trump's financial pledge and planned overhaul becomes a reality.

But Trump, in a social media post after the meeting, warned that he won't move forward with the renovations ‒ which he would pay for with his own money ‒ unless the judge's decision blocking his name from being attached to the building is overturned. The Justice Department has appealed the decision.

"If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place," Trump said.

When asked to respond to Beatty's claims about the board meeting, the White House did not deny the congresswoman's account.

"For decades, Democrats let the Kennedy Center rot as water damage spread, infrastructure crumbled, and a national treasure fell apart under their watch," White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said. " President Trump did what Democrats wouldn't by finally committing the resources and the leadership needed to restore the Kennedy Center and make it the finest performing arts facility in the world."

Recounting the board meeting, Beatty said Trump touted his career as a developer and told her that she had "never done anything."

"So I reminded him that he had more bankruptcies than anybody in the room," Beatty said. "I mean, it really went there, because I was not going to let him ‒ he was there in his role as chairman of the board ‒ bully me, intimidate me, and the facts for themselves."

Beatty added: "He didn't win. He didn't get his vanity project. He didn't get his name on it for the second time, so now he's attacking folks."

articles.title: Washington’s new gun permit system moves ahead as one sheriff calls law ‘insane’
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - Washington’s new permit-to-purchase requirement for firearms is moving from the statehouse to implementation, with the Washington State...
articles.body:
Washington is implementing a new permit-to-purchase requirement for firearms, with the State Patrol building the system that will require state approval before buying a gun.

The permit requirement, effective May 1, 2027, will include fingerprints, proof of training, and a $126 application fee, with renewals costing $90 if submitted before expiration.

Franklin County Sheriff Jim Raymond criticizes the law as unconstitutional, arguing that it places an additional layer of government approval on law-abiding citizens who have already passed background checks.

(The Center Square) - Washington's new permit-to-purchase requirement for firearms is moving from the statehouse to implementation, with the Washington State Patrol now building the system that will require firearm buyers to obtain state approval before purchasing a gun.

The permit requirement does not take effect until May 1, 2027, but work is already underway on the technology and processes needed to launch the program.

The agency says it is targeting early 2027 for the permit application and firearms-training certification systems so applicants have time to obtain permits before the law becomes mandatory.

That development is drawing renewed criticism from Franklin County Sheriff Jim Raymond, who says the law goes too far and could ultimately face a constitutional challenge.

"I think this is insane," Raymond said in a phone interview Wednesday with The Center Square.

Raymond said he believes the new permit requirement is unconstitutional because law-abiding Americans already have a constitutional right to keep and bear arms.

His criticism centers on what he sees as another layer of government approval for people who have already passed existing background checks.

"It's another level of control," Raymond said.

The permit application itself will include fingerprints, proof of the required training and an application fee. The law allows the State Patrol to charge fees intended to cover the direct and indirect costs of administering the permit program. The Legislature's bill report outlines the permit's five-year validity and fee structure.

The new permit-to-purchase application will cost $126 — a $90 permit fee plus a $36 fingerprint-processing fee. Local law enforcement agencies may also charge an additional fee to collect fingerprints. The permit will be valid for five years.

Renewals will cost $90 if submitted before the permit expires. A renewal filed within 90 days after expiration will cost an additional $25 late fee.

Under RCW 9.41.121 , which stemmed from House Bill 1163 that was signed by Gov. Bob Ferguson on May 20, 2025, Washington residents will have to obtain a five-year permit before purchasing or transferring a firearm beginning May 1, 2027.

"Gun violence in Washington state breaks apart too many families and kills too many children," Ferguson said after the signing . "We must put commonsense reforms into place that save lives."

The legislation was championed by gun safety organizations such as the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions.

"Washington's new law reflects the commitment of local advocates to a public health approach to gun violence prevention," said Kelly Roskam, director of law and policy at the Center, in a statement after the signing. "Firearm Purchaser Licensing is one of the most effective tools we have for reducing gun deaths."

Applicants will have to submit fingerprints through their local law enforcement agency, have completed a certified firearms safety training course within the previous five years, and pay the required fees. Washington law spells out the application and fingerprint requirements.

The new permit system will operate in addition to Washington's existing firearm background-check requirements and waiting period.

Raymond questioned why the state needs another process for people who are already legally eligible to own firearms.

"It's hard to respond to some of these stupid laws they try to pass nowadays," Raymond said.

He argued that criminals who are already willing to break the law are unlikely to be deterred by another permitting requirement.

"People that aren't law-abiding are going to figure out other ways to purchase firearms," Raymond said.

Raymond said he believes the policy places the burden primarily on law-abiding gun owners rather than addressing people who use firearms to commit crimes.

"People cause problems, not weapons themselves," he said.

The sheriff said he has supported some firearm-safety efforts, including classes offered through his own office. But he views the permit-to-purchase requirement differently.

Raymond said his concern is not limited to the training requirement. Instead, he objects to requiring someone to obtain government permission before making a purchase that he believes is protected by the Constitution.

The law could face scrutiny over its Second Amendment implications. The U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen established a historical-tradition framework for evaluating firearm regulations.

For now, Washington is moving forward with implementation. There are no current legal challenges to RCW 9.41.121 in the courts.

Beginning May 1, state law will prohibit a dealer from delivering a firearm unless the purchaser has a valid permit, has been cleared through the state background-check program and has satisfied the applicable waiting-period requirements.

Raymond, who has only a few months remaining in office, said his opposition to the law will not change his department's responsibility to enforce the law while continuing to defend constitutional rights.

He said the Franklin County Sheriff's Office will continue doing what it can to protect the rights of residents.

"All law enforcement believe in the Constitution and hold to it," Raymond said.

articles.title: Lula x Flávio Bolsonaro: Datafolha aponta empate técnico no 1º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta (17) aponta empate técnico entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro. Levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S. Paulo.
articles.summary: Diferença entre eles está dentro do intervalo da margem de erro da pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17).
articles.body:
Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) estão tecnicamente empatados na disputa pela presidência no 1º turno, segundo pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17), a duas semanas da votação.

Lula tem 39% das intenções de voto, mesmo índice registrado na semana passada.

Flávio aparece com 36% , após oscilar um ponto para cima (tinha 35%).

A diferença de três pontos está dentro do intervalo da margem de erro, que é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos. Entenda o que é margem de erro .

Em agosto, Lula tinha seis pontos de vantagem para Flávio Bolsonaro.

Há empate técnico também no 2º turno : 46% para Lula e 44% para Flávio.

Os dois candidatos empatam no índice de rejeição : 47% para cada um.

O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo.

Veja os números da pesquisa estimulada do 1º turno , em que o Datafolha mostra aos eleitores os nomes dos candidatos. Entre parênteses, o resultado da pesquisa anterior, do dia 11 de setembro .

O Datafolha ouviu 2.002 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 15 e 16 de setembro. A margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro no TSE é BR-04029/2026.

Nos votos válidos , quando o Datafolha exclui votos em branco, nulos e indecisos, Lula tem 43% e Flávio, 39%.

Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos e Romeu Zema — Foto: Globo

O Datafolha mostra também que 76% dos eleitores estão totalmente decididos sobre a escolha do candidato a presidente, e que 24% ainda podem mudar o voto. Entre os eleitores de Lula, 84% já estão decididos. Esse índice é de 82% no grupo que declara voto em Flávio Bolsonaro.

Veja agora os números da pesquisa espontânea , em que o Datafolha não mostra os nomes dos candidatos aos eleitores. A parcela de indecisos encolheu de 32% para 21% desde agosto.

articles.summary: Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas apresentou propostas para a saúde pública no estado.
articles.body:
Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz participou de sabatina promovida por portais de notícia em Manaus. — Foto: Reprodução/Amazonas Atual

O candidato ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz ( PSD ), participou de uma sabatina promovida por um conglomerado de portais de noticiais, em Manaus . Durante o compromisso, nesta quinta-feira (17), prometeu a construção de hospitais de alta e média complexidade no interior do estado.

Omar Aziz disputa o cargo pela coligação "Força Amazonas", formada pelo Partido Social Democrático (PSD), Movimento Democrático Brasileiro (MDB) e Republicanos. O candidato já foi governador do estado entre 2010 e 2014 e, posteriormente, foi eleito senador e reeleito ao cargo em 2022.

Questionado sobre projetos voltados à saúde, Omar criticou a falta de novos hospitais construídos no estado pelas gestões anteriores. Ele prometeu a criação de novas maternidades na capital e sete hospitais regionais em municípios estratégicos.

"O último hospital construído no Amazonas foi eu como governador. O último. De lá pra cá não construiram mais nenhum. Em Manaus, nós precisamos fazer três maternidades urgentes. [...] Eu tenho que fazer sete hospitais regionais de alta e média complexidade no interior. É inadmissível uma cidade como Itacoatiara não ter um hospital para que pegue aquela região do baixo Amazonas. Em Parintins, por exemplo, nós vamos fazer um hospital regional de 150 leitos", afirmou.

A agenda do candidato continuou pela tarde com viagem a município da Região Metropolitana de Manaus, onde participa de evento popular durante a noite.

articles.title: Em live, Flávio Bolsonaro diz que vai para recrutar 'fiscais de urna' | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PL à Presidência afirmou que atitude prevê evitar que "pessoas mal-intencionadas votem no lugar de outras". Desde a primeira eleição com urnas eletrônicas, nunca houve um caso de fraude no equipamento.
articles.summary: Candidato do PL disse que atitude prevê evitar ações de "pessoas mal-intencionadas". Desde a primeira eleição com urnas eletrônicas, nunca houve um caso de fraude no equipamento.
articles.body:
Candidato do PL à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou que irá recrutar pessoas para fazer a fiscalização das urnas eletrônicas no dia das eleições.

Em live na noite desta quinta-feira (17), o senador afirmou que ele precisa ter "gente nossa, pelo Brasil inteiro", para evitar que "pessoas mal-intencionadas votem no lugar de outras" -- o que não acontece nas eleições por uma série de ferramentas de segurança do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, como a biometria digital.

🔎 Desde a primeira eleição com urnas eletrônicas, nunca houve um caso de fraude no equipamento.

"A gente vai começar a fazer um trabalho de arregimentação de pessoas para nos ajudar na fiscalização no dia da eleição. Então, vamos divulgar os fiscais de urna", disse o candidato, que prometeu um site para a inscrição dos interessados.

"Basicamente, a gente vai recrutar as pessoas, [elas] vão poder se inscrever, vão ser credenciadas, vai ter um rápido ensinamento como é que faz para a gente fazer a fiscalização das urnas, em especial no momento em que a urna fechou. A gente tem que ter gente nossa, pelo Brasil inteiro, fiscalizando para evitar que pessoas mal-intencionadas votem no lugar de outras e façam alguns tipos de atitudes ilegais como essas aí", sem dar exemplos de malfeitos.

Em julho deste ano, Flávio Bolsonaro atacou as urnas eletrônicas durante reunião com diplomatas com acusações já desmentidas pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral. O senador repetiu atitude de seu pai, Jair Bolsonaro, que em julho de 2022 atacou o sistema eleitoral , afirmando, sem provas, que as urnas não seriam seguras.

Flávio Bolsonaro durante live nesta quinta-feira, 17 de setembro — Foto: Reprodução

Antes de cada eleição, o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) promove uma série de testes públicos para tentar identificar falhas nos sistemas eleitorais.

Um exemplo é o chamado Teste de Segurança, iniciativa que permite a especialistas em computação e a qualquer cidadão brasileiro maior de 18 anos tentar encontrar vulnerabilidades nos sistemas usados nas urnas eletrônicas.

Um dos principais alvos dos testes é o código-fonte dos sistemas da urna. É o conjunto de instruções que determina como o software deve funcionar. Segundo o TSE, desde a primeira edição do teste, em 2009, nenhum participante conseguiu encontrar uma falha capaz de comprometer o sigilo do voto ou o resultado de uma eleição.

O teste público de segurança é apenas um dos mecanismos de verificação usados pela Justiça Eleitoral. Confira as principais etapas do processo:

Um ano antes da eleição, os códigos-fonte dos sistemas eleitorais são abertos para análise. Entidades autorizadas podem examinar os códigos, acompanhar o funcionamento dos sistemas e solicitar esclarecimentos ao TSE.

Mais próximo da votação, as urnas que serão utilizadas passam por um processo de assinatura digital e lacração. A partir desse momento, qualquer alteração nos programas pode ser identificada.

No dia da eleição, algumas urnas são sorteadas para passar pelo teste de integridade. Na véspera, representantes de entidades e partidos preenchem cédulas de papel com votos e as depositam em uma urna de lona. No dia da votação, os mesmos votos são digitados na urna eletrônica sorteada para o teste — todo o processo é acompanhado e filmado.

Ao final, é feita a comparação entre o resultado registrado pela urna eletrônica e os votos preenchidos nas cédulas de papel. É assim que se verifica, na prática, se o equipamento registra e contabiliza corretamente os votos.

Antes do início da votação, cada urna emite a chamada "zerésima", documento que comprova que o equipamento começou o dia sem nenhum voto registrado.

Ao final da votação, a urna emite o boletim de urna, com os totais de votos recebidos por cada candidato e partido, além dos votos brancos e nulos. Uma cópia do boletim é afixada na seção eleitoral, e o documento traz um QR Code que pode ser lido por qualquer pessoa, permitindo comparar o resultado daquela urna com os dados publicados posteriormente pelo TSE.

articles.standfirst: Candidato à Presidência entrou com ação contra medida após ministro André Mendonça rejeitar ação de Zé Trovão por considerar que o deputado não possui "legitimidade" para o questionamento. Com o reajuste, piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691.
articles.summary: Candidato à Presidência entrou com ação contra medida após ministro André Mendonça rejeitar ação de Zé Trovão por considerar que o deputado não possui "legitimidade" para o questionamento. Com o reajuste,  piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691.
articles.body:
O candidato à Presidência Renan Santos (Missão) entrou com uma representação no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) contra o reajuste do Bolsa Família anunciado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) nesta quinta-feira (15) .

Com o reajuste, o piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691 .

Mais cedo, o ministro André Mendonça rejeitou uma ação em que o deputado federal e candidato à reeleição Zé Trovão (PL-SC) , aliado do senador e candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), questionava o reajuste.

Mendonça, sorteado relator do caso no TSE, mencionou decisões anteriores segundo as quais um candidato a deputado federal não tem legitimidade para apresentar uma ação contra um candidato à Presidência da República, uma vez que os dois cargos são disputados em circunscrições eleitorais diferentes.

O ministro André Mendonça deve assumir a relatoria do pedido do partido Missão por prevenção, ou seja, porque já tinha sob sua relatoria um caso anterior semelhante.

O candidato à Presidência pediu a concessão de liminar para sustar os efeitos do decreto que prevê o reajuste, até a posse dos candidatos eleitos neste ano, "para resguardar a isonomia e a paridade entre os candidatos".

Na ação, Renan Santos alega finalidade eleitoral na medida e que o objetivo é "evitar o desvio de finalidade e a repercussão da medida governamental eleitoreira adotada no desequilíbrio do pleito.

O anúncio ocorreu na manhã desta quinta no Palácio do Planalto. Desde que foi relançado em março de 2023 pelo governo petista, o Bolsa Família estava sem correção.

Com o reajuste, o piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691. O novo valor começa a valer no mês de outubro, com pagamentos a partir do dia 19, entre o primeiro e o segundo turno (se houver) das eleições presidenciais.

Segundo o Ministério do Planejamento, o custo do reajuste do Bolsa Família neste ano será de R$ 5,8 bilhões. Para 2027, o impacto nas despesas será de R$ 22,7 bilhões.

Em agosto, o governo enviou ao Legislativo a proposta de orçamento para 2027 sem contemplar aumento nos valores do programa.

O Ministério da Fazenda informou que o reajuste do Bolsa Família apenas repõe as perdas inflacionárias dos últimos anos, o que não equivaleria a um aumento do benefício social.

O ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, negou que a medida tenha relação com as eleições de 2026.

De acordo com a Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), a lei que instituiu o novo Bolsa Família, em 2023, autoriza o Poder Executivo a "corrigir os valores dos benefícios e proíbe sua redução".

articles.title: Araceli Lemos propõe cobrar devedores fiscais  | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidata do PSOL ao Governo do Estado participou de encontro com representantes de movimentos de mulheres em Belém nesta quinta-feira, 17.
articles.summary: Candidata do PSOL ao Governo do Estado cumpriu agenda de campanha com representantes de movimentos de mulheres em Belém, nesta quinta-feira, 17.
articles.body:
A candidata do PSOL ao Governo do Pará, Araceli Lemos, disse nesta quinta-feira (17) que pretende cobrar débitos fiscais de grandes empresas para criar um fundo destinado a financiar educação, inovação e geração de renda, com prioridade para mulheres chefes de família.

"Nós vamos fazer com que aqueles que não estão pagando paguem o que devem para que o estado tenha mais recursos", afirmou.

Araceli participou de um encontro na sede do Partido Socialismo e Liberdade (PSOL), no bairro de São Brás, em Belém, para debater a rede de proteção às mulheres. Acompanhada da candidata a vice-governadora, Fátima Santana, ela apresentou propostas do plano de governo a representantes de movimentos de mulheres da capital.

Durante a agenda, a candidata defendeu o combate ao feminicídio, a instalação de delegacias especializadas com funcionamento 24 horas em todos os municípios do estado e a implantação de um programa de prevenção à violência contra a mulher.

Para financiar as propostas, Araceli afirmou que pretende cobrar dívidas tributárias, fazer uma auditoria nas isenções fiscais e reduzir despesas que a campanha considera excessivas. A candidata citou especialmente grandes empresas dos setores mineral e do agronegócio.

Segundo Araceli, um levantamento usado pela campanha aponta que uma única empresa teria cerca de R$ 2 bilhões em débitos com o estado. Ela não identificou a empresa durante a agenda.

"Nós vamos fazer uma verdadeira auditoria nas isenções fiscais, porque nós achamos importantes as isenções para aqueles que geram emprego e que pagam seus impostos", declarou.

A candidata estima obter cerca de R$ 10 bilhões a partir de diferentes medidas. Além da cobrança de débitos e da revisão de isenções, ela citou redução de gastos com publicidade e eventos e valores que, segundo a campanha, estariam relacionados a obras superfaturadas.

Araceli não detalhou como chegou à estimativa de R$ 10 bilhões.

"Nós temos condições de arrecadar valores aproximados a R$ 10 bilhões para estar investindo em melhoria das condições das mulheres no estado do Pará", afirmou.

Questionada sobre a criação do fundo, Araceli disse que a medida dependerá de aprovação da Assembleia Legislativa do Pará (Alepa). Segundo a candidata, uma proposta semelhante apresentada por ela quando era deputada estadual foi rejeitada.

"Agora será um projeto do Executivo para a Assembleia Legislativa", disse.

articles.summary: Um homem de 29 anos foi preso em flagrante nesta quinta-feira (17) em Presidente Prudente (SP). Ele é suspeito de esfaquear o pai para defender sua cadela.

Homem é preso suspeito de tentativa de homicídio após agredir o pai por causa de cadela em Prudente — Foto: Reprodução/Polícia Civil

Um homem de 29 anos foi preso em flagrante suspeito de esfaquear o pai, de 67 anos, para defender sua cadela de estimação de agressões nesta quinta-feira (17), em Presidente Prudente (SP). O crime ocorreu em uma residência no Conjunto Habitacional Augusto de Paula.

Ao chegarem ao local da ocorrência, os policiais militares constataram que o animal estava ferido e apreenderam uma faca quebrada usada no ataque. Em depoimento, o jovem admitiu ter golpeado o pai com o objeto cortante para cessar as agressões contra o animal.

A vítima foi socorrida, levada para o Hospital Regional e pediu uma medida protetiva contra o filho. O estado de saúde não foi divulgado.

O caso foi registrado na Delegacia de Plantão de Presidente Prudente como tentativa de homicídio por motivo fútil. A cadela recebeu socorro por apresentar ferimentos, mas não há novas atualizações sobre o seu estado de saúde.

articles.title: Trump’s frustration hits a boiling point with loss after loss
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh announced an interest rate hike after Trump spent months demanding large cuts.
articles.body:
Donald Trump is boiling with frustration after a spate of political blows weakened his presumption of dominance in Washington and abroad.

It's been one of those tough weeks that presidents sometimes suffer, when multiple priorities seem to unravel all at once.

The Supreme Court's decision to block Trump's plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms left him fuming at his first-term appointees on the top bench, whom he slammed as "a shell" of their former selves.

A lower court again frustrated Trump's bid to renovate the Kennedy Center. The drama over the arts citadel, which Trump now plans to shut down , is most damaging because it's an unflattering character reveal. Everyone knows this is really about him trying to muscle his own name onto the living memorial to an assassinated president.

The president's authority took another dent Tuesday when the GOP-led House voted to require him to end his war with Iran , as three more Republicans swelled the list of party heretics to seven.

Trump's big midterm offer of a $5,000 check for every American if Republicans win in November, meanwhile, looks dead in the water after Capitol Hill GOPers distanced themselves from the idea. And Speaker Mike Johnson, a close Trump ally, chose to send House lawmakers home Wednesday — a day earlier than planned — to avoid a potentially embarrassing vote on whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Wednesday brought another implied rebuke to Trump when the Federal Reserve, under Trump's handpicked new Chair Kevin Warsh, raised interest rates for the first time since July 2023 in a sign of central bank independence. Trump has spent months demanding large cuts to the cost of borrowing, ignoring the specter of rising inflation that his trade and war policies exacerbated.

The president reacted to the Fed's move with a new outburst of exasperation on Truth Social . He advanced his idiosyncratic economic assessment that the country is booming and therefore US rates should be at 1%, rather than the new benchmark in the range of 3.75% to 4%.

Trump's vision of unchallenged US power abroad is also being undermined.

In a stunning development, Canada, a third of the mighty North American trading bloc, was just offered associate membership in another group, the European Union, as it seeks new friends following Trump's sovereignty threats and tariff attacks.

And Trump's waffling over when the Iran war will end can't cover up a worsening situation. Tehran-backed Houthi rebels just seized land in and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait , potentially giving them leverage over another critical oil exporting route while the US is still struggling to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The president's cascade of misfortunes this week collectively point to more than the typical political dings for second-term presidents.

Each arises from a big, risky Trump bet and an apparently over-optimistic assessment of his own personal and political power.

He bitterly rebuked Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett for appearing to be part of the majority that blocked his bid to sow chaos over postal ballots ahead of the midterms. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social. His critique is revealing because it shows a belief that his appointees would adjudicate the law in a way that repaid a personal debt to the president.

Democrats gripe about a Supreme Court that has often shared Trump's vision of expansive executive authority. But at times, these three justices have also reined in Trump's power. These are turbulent times, but it shouldn't be surprising when Supreme Court justices uphold the Constitution, which gives control of elections to the states. Their lifetime tenure also means they'll be forging their own legacies long after Trump leaves office.

Trump's disagreement with the Fed's rate hike was not a surprise. But it is another sign that his authority is limited. After all, he'd spent months hounding Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell over his failure to slash rates. Now the man he picked as a replacement has overseen a rate increase.

Trump has perhaps done more than any other president to erode the constraints on executive power imposed by the Constitution and custom. He has found particular success, for instance, in his evisceration of parts of the federal government by acting with shock and awe to outpace initial court action.

But the Kennedy Center farce, the mail-in voting decision and Fed independence are important indicators. They show that even faced with a relentless president, some institutions of government are standing firm.

Trump has dominated the Republican Party for a decade. But his inability to maintain unanimous support over a constitutionally questionable war; his failure to browbeat the Senate into passing his voter registration bill; and lawmakers' coolness to his $5,000 giveaway idea suggest cracks are emerging in his power base.

Canada's overtures to the EU represent an extraordinary geopolitical shock. The second Trump administration made US hegemony over the Western Hemisphere an article of faith. But the country's closest geographical and cultural ally is seeking a highly symbolic break with its "America First" neighbor, a sign it now feels more politically and morally aligned with Europe.

Trump said Wednesday that the US could put "heavy tariffs" on the European Union if it allowed Canada to become its first "associate member" and if he considers it a "hostile act."

"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility," he told reporters.

It's unclear what associate membership of the EU means and how it would alter Canada's huge trade relationship with the US if the current tariff war ends. But it's clear Trump's "51st state" threats led Ottawa to conclude it cannot depend on Washington even when Trump leaves office. A weaker North American trade relationship and fractured alliance system will ultimately weaken Washington's ability to project unified Western power.

Equally, the Iran conflict is chipping away at the administration's conceit that the US is so powerful it can do exactly as it wants.

The president can't say whether the war will end before or after the midterms. Iran's armed forces might be crushed and its economy in free fall. But Tehran's revolutionary regime is as entrenched as ever nearly eight months into a war in which it defied a superpower.

So how will Trump's week of big reversals alter his political position, play into the midterms and set the tone for whatever new balance of Washington power emerges from election season?

One obvious takeaway is that political gravity may be reasserting itself. The Iran war defections show that Trump is not immune from the ritual of endangered lawmakers seeking distance from an unpopular president.

"Where we agree with the president, we're going to fight with him. Where we disagree with the president on things like beef, on tariffs, on the current state of how operations are working in Iran, we're going to call him out and have a conversation on that," Iowa Rep. Zach Nunn, who voted for an end to the war Tuesday, told CNN's Manu Raju.

This is a bad midterm omen. Nunn is obviously reacting to voter sentiment in a solid Trump state. His plight suggests the Republican foundation is weakening.

Trump's susceptibility to ordinary political forces is significant because the vibe last year was that he was all but unstoppable; that he had obliterated every guardrail and could compel elite law firms, corporate executives and university presidents to genuflect.

This is not to say that Trump is an exhausted force. He's long defied pundits predicting his political demise. He engineered the greatest comeback in American history less than two years ago.

And if Democrats win back the House or the Senate in the midterms, Trump could paradoxically find new political definition. Any Democratic overreach during a promised blizzard of probes into the White House or an ideological dive left would offer an opening to a political street fighter who is most effective with a foil.

But a week in which power has tangibly ebbed from a president with an approval rating in the 30s can't be ignored.

Once an aura of invincibility fades, political authority can erode quickly.

articles.title: 20 states sue to block Trump admin rule that would make it harder for immigrants to obtain visas, green cards
articles.summary: More than 20 states sued the Department of Homeland Security over a public charge rule that could increase green card denials based on Medicaid and SNAP use.
articles.body:
More than 20 states are suing the Trump administration over a new Department of Homeland Security rule expanding the list of government aid that could disqualify immigrants from obtaining visas or green cards.

The rule, set to take effect on Friday, would allow immigration officials to consider an immigrant's use of benefits like Medicaid and SNAP when determining their likelihood of becoming dependent on government aid.

The states' and cities' lawsuits aim to declare the rule unlawful and prevent DHS from using it, arguing that the new rule is arbitrary and exceeds the agency's authority.

More than 20 states are suing the Trump administration over a new Department of Homeland Security rule that would give immigration officials wider discretion in determining what constitutes a public charge, a statute that allows the government to deny visas or green cards to applicants it determines are likely to become dependent on government assistance.

The rule, which is set to take effect on Friday, would expand the list of possible government aid that officials could point to when deciding to disqualify an applicant.

New York State Attorney General Letitia James led a coalition of 21 states and Washington, D.C., in suing the administration over what they describe as punishment for immigrants' lawful use of public assistance. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani led a separate lawsuit filed by a coalition of cities challenging DHS' rule.

James said the rule would allow immigration officials to consider an immigrant's use of benefits like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and participation in school meal programs when determining whether they could become dependent on government aid. She also said it could lead to more fear of interacting with the government for people who are part of an immigrant family.

"Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported," James said in a statement. "This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled. My office fought this exact policy once before and won, and we are leading the nation to ensure the Trump administration cannot inflict this harm on families again."

The public charge ground applies to certain immigrants seeking admission or adjustment of status. Most undocumented immigrants are ineligible for federal means-tested public benefits, although limited exceptions exist under federal and state law.

The states argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants pull from programs over fears about the public charge rule.

Immigration officials under the Biden administration's 2022 public charge rule generally considered only cash assistance for income maintenance, such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), along with government-funded long-term institutionalization, when determining a public charge.

The rule does not specify a fixed list of public benefits that immigration officials may consider. Instead, it states that officers may consider the receipt of any means-tested public benefits as part of a public charge determination, giving them broader discretion in evaluating applicants.

The states' and cities' lawsuits asked the courts to declare the rule unlawful and prevent DHS from using it.

"It's very hard to predict how courts will look at this issue. It is very unusual regulation though," Cato Institute Director of Immigration Studies David Bier told Fox News Digital. "I think from that standpoint, the states have a good argument that we had a well-defined public charge rule and the administration didn't replace it with some other well-defined rule, it replaced it with nothing. So now there's just discretion to the officers to do whatever they want with the underlying statute. There's no regulation that clearly says this is what it means to be a public charge in the United States."

"The rule as it was before this new regulation was you had to be primarily dependent on certain government benefit programs. This rule removes that definition and doesn't replace it with anything. So now people and applicants, lawyers who are applying to the government on behalf of applicants, they don't know really what the law is," he continued.

The states' lawsuit argues that DHS is exceeding its authority because Congress did not approve a broader interpretation of what it means to be a public charge. The states say the new rule is arbitrary and that the agency ignored the harmful consequences of the change.

"Cruelty is the point," James said at a press conference on Monday. "Having a chilling effect on immigrants is the point. Letting individuals know that they are not welcome here is the point. Immigration animus is the point. The fact that you're going to deny individuals who are sick and hungry and homeless benefits just is beyond the pale."

DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

Bier said the rule does not prohibit immigrants from receiving welfare and is only used as an officer's projection about someone's likelihood of future welfare use in the U.S., warning that it could lead to self-sufficient applicants being denied.

"Whether someone is currently using benefits or not doesn't matter under this evaluation. It's this probabilistic determination of the future that they're using in order to deny people legal status and legal permanent resident status in the United States. That's a much more difficult assessment to make. That's going to result in arbitrary denials. It's just not possible to do this type of assessment and not result in people who would be self-sufficient being denied status," he said.

This comes as President Donald Trump pursues a broader immigration crackdown that has extended beyond illegal immigration to legal immigration pathways. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on curbing illegal immigration, his administration has also imposed additional restrictions on legal immigration, including higher fees for certain work visas and new limits on how long some foreign students and journalists can remain in the U.S.

The administration has also pursued visa revocations and removal proceedings in cases involving political activity and speech, including some anti-Israel activists. Those efforts have prompted court challenges in which plaintiffs allege violations of First Amendment free speech and Fifth Amendment due process protections.

"It's very clear that this administration wants to restrict both illegal immigration, which obviously it's done at the border, and through deportations, but also legal immigration," Bier said.

Last month, the administration directed U.S. embassies and consulates around the world to postpone immigrant visa interviews while consular officers complete training on new public charge guidance, temporarily stalling applications that had reached the interview stage.

"The primary population that's going to be affected by this public charge rule are spouses of U.S. citizens and their kids who are trying to receive green cards so they can live with their American spouse or parent here in the United States. That's the overwhelming majority of the people who are going to be affected by the rule. It's going to result in many of those immigrant families being separated from their American spouse or parent," Bier said.

The public charge provision stems from the Immigration Act of 1882, when federal lawmakers sought to ensure that immigrants would be able to take care of themselves and not become a public burden.

After years of only considering cash benefits, the first Trump administration widened the categories of benefit programs that could be considered a public charge, including Medicaid, food stamps and housing vouchers. But the Biden administration in 2022 published a rule that returned to the previous guidance. The rule set to take effect this week would rescind the Biden administration's rule.

The new rule is broader than the one from the first Trump administration, as it does not specify which safety nets should be considered and only states that DHS "will consider the receipt of any means-tested public benefits."

"One of the most important things to understand is that during the first Trump administration, they had a public charge rule that was well defined that really did explain exactly what you were supposed to do in order to not be deemed a public charge or who was a public charge. This is completely different from that. It's essentially the Wild West. No one knows what's going on; no one knows what the law is now," Bier said.

articles.title: Zuckerberg, Musk And Huang Reportedly Convinced Trump To Block AI Regulator
articles.summary: Zuckerberg and Huang have recently opposed calls to slow down frontier AI development while Musk has backed a push by Amodei to pace advancements until
articles.body:
Billionaire tech CEOs Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang spoke with President Donald Trump last month and convinced him to block efforts to establish an AI industry-funded regulator, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, despite growing fears about AI safety.

Citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter, the Journal reported Meta's Zuckerberg, SpaceXAI's Musk and Nvidia's Huang opposed a push by some AI executives to build an industry-funded oversight body similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

The proposal for a FINRA-style AI regulatory and standards body came from Google's Chief Scientist Demis Hassabis, who also chairs the tech giant's DeepMind AI unit.

The billionaires' purported concern about the proposal stemmed from fears it would entrench more power in the hands of the three leading American AI labs: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's DeepMind.

All three expressed their concerns to Trump in separate conversations, after which the president didn't move forward with proposals for setting up the regulator.

According to the Journal, administration officials have told top AI executives that building consensus on an AI regulatory framework at the White House is challenging because CEOs opposing such moves are contacting Trump directly.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Huang are expected to attend next week's State Dinner at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping. Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook, who recently stepped down as CEO but remained on the board as the company's government liaison, will also be in attendance. Despite Trump's recent dismissal of AI safety fears and push to beat China, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios that the Trump administration is "open to discussions on avoiding shared risks" on the issue.

What Has Zuckerberg Said About AI Safety Recently?

On Tuesday, both Zuckerberg and Huang downplayed concerns about AI safety risks and argued that companies can pace themselves without external regulation. Zuckerberg outlined his argument in a lengthy X post , arguing that companies have a "strong natural incentive" to ensure AI is aligned to safety and human interests, as people will not use AI agents that are "misaligned with them and…don't do what they ask." Meta's billionaire CEO also appeared to dismiss the argument that AI companies may need to coordinate to ensure safety, noting that "every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens." Zuckerberg, however, said his company was open to engaging independent evaluators and advisers on AI, agreeing with Anthropic and OpenAI.

What Has Huang Said About AI Safety Recently?

Huang also dismissed slowdown talks and safety fears on Tuesday, telling attendees at Salesforce's annual Dreamforce event that the question of having to choose between safety and speed was a "false" one. "You could definitely have both at the same time." He then argued: "We don't need new laws — we don't need new regulations." Huang then pointed to market forces and said companies should pace themselves until they are confident about "releasing something that the market would appreciate." A day earlier, he had attended a call from Trump while he was live on stage during the All-In Summit. In the call, Trump argued that people opposing AI and data center construction were "playing right into the hands" of skeptics and China and declared, "We're not going to let that happen." Huang told the president, "You're right. We're not going to let that happen, sir."

What Has Musk Said About AI Safety Recently?

Last week, Musk questioned and mocked a series of viral X posts made by Jacob Coxon, an ex-Anthropic researcher, who quit the company and raised alarm about AI-driven human extinction over the next decade. Musk said the posts seemed like a 'setup and argued that this was a spark that followed "groundwork" for a "psy op (for lack of a better term)," presumably against AI. But when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued warnings about AI safety and called for "pacing" the development of frontier AI models and better coordination on safety, Musk wrote, " Dario is right ." However, unlike Anthropic and OpenAI, Musk's SpaceXAI has not laid out any plans to coordinate or pace frontier AI model development.

articles.title: Massie: GOP leaders found ‘other Republicans’ who would join Hegseth impeachment push
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) argued Wednesday that House GOP leaders sent the lower chamber home early because they found other Republicans in support of his p...
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) argued Wednesday that House GOP leaders sent the lower chamber home early because they found other Republicans in support of his push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

"The fact that they didn't vote on it tells me that they did a whip check, and they probably found that there were some other Republicans, besides me, that were going to vote for this, or at least didn't want to be on the record supporting Hegseth," he told host Kaitlan Collins on CNN's "The Source."

The outgoing Kentucky libertarian, a frequent critic of President Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday.

Massie accused Hegseth of violating his "oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States," citing his handling of the Iran war and operations to kill alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.

The GOP lawmaker, who lost his primary in May to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein, also made his impeachment resolution privileged.

That would have forced lawmakers to vote on it within two days, before Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent them home a day early for a seven-week recess.

Given that, Massie argued the early recess was because of his impeachment resolution.

"I know it was," he told Collins, adding it is "actually bad politics" to have the resolution "hanging over Pete Hegseth's head" until the House returns in November.

"If there was any other reason that they canceled tomorrow's day of session, they could have had the Hegseth vote tonight," the GOP lawmaker added. "Because the rules say that he has to have the vote within 48 hours. They don't … say he has to wait 48 hours."

"So, [Johnson] could have had the vote yesterday, as soon as I introduced the articles. He could have done it today, before he adjourned Congress," he added, later dubbing the early recess the "Hegseth holiday."

articles.title: The Latest: Federal judge orders Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice of any building changes
articles.summary: A federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolis...
articles.body:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major physical changes to the building , including demolishing it, as President Donald Trump has threatened.

Trump said Wednesday that without his efforts to restore the aging building, "it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down." Earlier on Thursday, a top official at the Kennedy Center said he closed the iconic performing arts center temporarily due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the building.

The U.S. is putting further pressure on Iran this week, hoping to disrupt Tehran's attempts to evade U.S. sanctions and economic pressure levied by the Trump administration . The U.S. is going after digital currency networks it says are illegally providing sanctioned Iranian entities with access to the international financial system.

Trump is withdrawing his nomination of Lance Schroyer to lead U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the White House said Thursday. The step ensures that an agency at the forefront of Trump's domestic agenda will remain without a Senate-confirmed leader for at least a while longer.

Postal Service chief says work stopped on system key to Trump effort to limit mail voting

The U.S. Postal Service has stopped developing the controversial computer system after the Supreme Court rejected Trump's executive order this week.

Postmaster General David Steiner confirmed the halt Thursday. He emphasized the agency's independence and operational focus.

Trump's order aimed to create state citizenship lists for mail voting, but the system faced criticism that it was riddled with errors. A memo to postal employees stated the agency won't enforce new rules for the 2026 election. Despite the halt, concerns remain about postmark delays affecting mail-in ballots. Steiner urged voters to submit ballots early.

Trump signs executive orders designed to expand hunting and fishing

The pair of orders seek to expand fresh and saltwater fishing while giving the secretary of the interior and other federal agencies 90 days to find ways to expand hunting, including of species not subject to certain endangered protection laws.

Those agencies will have 180 days to propose modifications to federal restrictions against hunting and fishing on federal land and to find ways to expand using that land for recreation.

Trump's order also seeks to authorize the use of "assistive technology on access trails and hunting locations" and permit using "traditional lead ammunition and tackle."

Trump signed the orders privately but is hosting an evening gathering in the White House's Rose Garden that will feature 100-plus invited hunters, anglers and outdoor industry leaders.

Russia and China halt US proposal on Iran sanctions at the UN

The United Nations resolution from the United States would have authorized U.N. experts to keep monitoring sanctions that were reimposed against Iran over its nuclear program.

The U.N. Security Council sanctions remain in effect after Thursday's vote. There was a "snapback" last year of the sanctions that freeze Iran's assets abroad, halt arms deals with Tehran and penalize any development of Iran's ballistic missile program, among other measures.

The United States had drafted a resolution to extend the mandate of a U.N. expert panel monitoring the sanctions, but it was defeated by the Russian and Chinese vetoes.

U.S. deputy ambassador to the U.N. Jennifer Locetta said the experts "would have shined the light" on prohibited cooperation between Iran and its partners.

US piles more pressure on Iran to disrupt sanctions evasion efforts

The Trump administration is stepping up efforts to combat Iranian attempts to circumvent U.S. sanctions.

The U.S. is now going after digital currency networks it says are illegally providing sanctioned Iranian entities with access to the international financial system.

The Treasury and State Departments announced on Thursday that they had targeted two companies and three individuals who have played a role in helping Iran evade sanctions.

The companies are Bitbank and the Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Company and three associates of BitBank's previously sanctioned chief Babak Zajani.

The move freezes any assets those affected may have in U.S. jurisdictions or that come into contact with U.S. financial institutions, bar Americans from doing business with them and could result in criminal action against foreign entities that violate the sanctions.

Data centers figure prominently in former interior secretary's campaign for New Mexico governor

Data centers are emerging as a flashpoint in New Mexico's governor's race with both major party candidates staking out positions on the rapidly growing industry.

Former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland vowed Thursday to place a moratorium on new large-scale data center construction in New Mexico if elected governor.

"The bottom line is we don't have water to waste," the Democrat said in Albuquerque.

Haaland's campaign said her proposed moratorium would not affect projects already underway but would remain until "strong, clear" regulations are enacted.

Campaign finance filings showed companies and executives tied to a massive Project Jupiter data center planned in southern New Mexico donated tens of thousands of dollars to Haaland's campaign.

Those interests didn't donate to GOP nominee Gregg Hull in the same period. Hull opposes a moratorium, arguing the state should compete to attract data center investment while regulating its environmental and other impacts.

Man accused of ties to bin Laden has 20-year Guantanamo detention reviewed

A man initially accused of being a high-profile al-Qaida figure appeared at a hearing Thursday at the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where he's been held without charges for 20 years.

A U.S. government official said at the detention review hearing that Abu Zubaydah had "probably" served as one of Osama bin Laden's most trusted facilitators.

The brief hearing offered a rare glimpse into the secretive military court proceedings of a suspect who had been tortured at CIA black sites during the U.S. war on terrorism. His case remains unresolved 25 years after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

The man's private attorney, Annika Conrad, acknowledged he had known bin Laden. But she said he never belonged to the militant group of the 9/11 mastermind. She argued Zubaydah poses no security threat to the U.S. and should be transferred out of Guantanamo.

White House slams finding from UN human rights body

The White House issued a scathing statement after experts commissioned by the U.N.'s top human rights body say they found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran.

"The UN Human Rights Council has accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Thursday.

She added: "The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region."

US approves visas for top Iranian officials for UN meetings in New York

The State Department says it had approved visas for Iran's "core delegation" and essential staffers.

The core delegation includes President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to U.S. officials who spoke on condition of anonymity due visa privacy laws.

The move is unusual due to the ongoing conflict between Iran and the United States and no sign that agreements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to talks on Iran's nuclear program are close.

And, according to the U.S. government, Iran remains the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism.

Senate blocks House-passed measure on data centers

The Senate has blocked a House-passed bill that aims to have data centers pay for their substantial energy needs.

Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio sought to pass the measure through unanimous consent. He's been facing attack ads on the issue as he seeks reelection and as people gather signatures in his state for a referendum to outright ban their construction.

The legislation that Husted sought to pass would require state utility regulators to consider a standard ensuring that data centers pay the full cost of the infrastructure needed to serve them.

"If you create the costs you should pay the costs," Husted said.

But Democratic Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico objected. Heinrich says the bill falls short of what's needed.

"Rather than voluntary pledges or suggestions to states, Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth," Heinrich said.

US OKs to $24 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia

The Trump administration's approval of the sale of the advanced warplanes to Saudi Arabia signals a boost in U.S. military cooperation with Gulf Arab states at a time when the war against Iran is at a stalemate.

The State Department said Thursday it has given the green light for the Saudis to purchase 48 F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter aircraft. Also included in the deal are jet engines, secure communication and navigational systems, spare parts and training.

The statement released by the State Department said the sale supports U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives by improving the security of a major non-NATO ally. It called Saudi Arabia "a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region."

Judge says Kennedy Center must give notice before making any major changes to building

The judge's order says the Kennedy Center must provide 30 days' notice before making significant changes to the building, including demolishing it as President Donald Trump has threatened.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said his ruling would "avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events."

Trump was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on the center's board.

He said Wednesday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, saying "if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape."

Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer as his nominee to lead ICE

The White House said Thursday that Trump is withdrawing its nomination of the former Oklahoma state trooper to lead U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The step ensures that an agency at the forefront of President Donald Trump's domestic agenda will remain without a Senate-confirmed leader for at least a while longer.

Schroyer is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former U.S. senator from Oklahoma. He has little experience with immigration.

The White House, in a brief statement, offered no comment on the decision.

When he nominated Schroyer in June, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that his pick was "a PATRIOT with real operational experience." Trump also called Schroyer a "proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst."

Appeals court considers a Missouri congressional map backed by Trump

The federal appeals court panel is weighing an attempt to revive Missouri congressional districts backed by President Donald Trump.

The U.S. Supreme Court blocked those districts from being used in the November election. But on Thursday, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments about whether the state should use the new Republican-drawn U.S. House districts.

It wasn't immediately clear what the impact would be, even if the panel were to rule in favor of the new map.

Local election officials are already printing ballots under the current districts. They face a Friday deadline to mail out absentee ballots to overseas citizens and military voters.

ICE officer charged in non-fatal shooting is arrested by Minnesota authorities

A federal immigration officer charged with shooting and wounding a Venezuelan man in January and lying about the circumstances to investigators was set to appear Thursday afternoon before a Minnesota judge.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro faces both state and federal charges stemming from the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis during a federal immigration crackdown in the Minneapolis area. Prosecutors say Castro falsely told investigators that he had been attacked with a broom and a shovel.

The Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension said in an online post that it arrested Castro on Wednesday in Minneapolis on an outstanding warrant charging him with assault and false reporting of a crime.

This item has been revised to correct the middle name of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

Man gets 14-month prison sentence for spraying US Rep Ilhan Omar with vinegar

The man who sprayed vinegar at U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday under an agreement with prosecutors.

Sentencing for Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan. 27 assault.

Authorities later determined he had sprayed the Democratic congresswoman from Minnesota with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He was charged with assaulting a U.S. officer.

During an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions. Omar was not hurt in the attack and continued the January town hall after the incident.

Kennedy Center closed temporarily to assess building's 'risks to public safety'

A top official at the Kennedy Center says he closed the iconic performing arts center temporarily due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the aging building.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, said in a court filing Thursday that the building will be closed for at least seven days to "assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration."

The temporary closure, which occurred without notice Wednesday, is separate from a vote

Tuesday by the Kennedy Center's board to close the performing arts center indefinitely for repairs. The closure may be extended after officials evaluate the center next week.

UN-backed experts cite possible US war crimes in Iran strikes

Human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.'s top human rights body say they've found "reasonable grounds" to believe the U.S. committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including one on a school in the southern city of Minab.

In a non-binding report published Thursday, they also accuse Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people.

The report adds to international evidence gathered about possible crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to pursue justice in international courts.

The fact-finding mission was created by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.'s top human rights body. The grouping of independent experts is expected to present their findings next week to the council, which is made up of 47 U.N. member countries.

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

House Democratic leader says Republicans are 'desperate' as MAGA, Inc. money flows for midterms

Hakeem Jeffries said Republicans have nothing left to offer voters than "trying to unload tens of millions of dollars" on the House, Senate and governors' races.

"But they can't even stick to their own brand," he said.

Jeffries pointed out that the Trump-affiliated group is creating "all of these other entities," which he suggested was so that they don't have to disclose MAGA Inc. as the spender in the races.

Jeffries said Democrats will have enough funding to defend their House incumbents and flip seats to take back the majority.

Former US Sen. Jon Kyl of Arizona, a 'workhorse' who shaped water policy, dies at 84

He also guided the confirmation of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

Kyl died Wednesday night from a neurological disorder, said Gordon James, a communications professional who is longtime friends with the Kyl family. Kyl had withdrawn from public life in December 2025 after announcing he'd been diagnosed with dementia .

Kyl spent almost three decades in Congress, serving in both chambers, and watched his party undergo a drastic transformation, with his career spanning Ronald Reagan's presidency to President Trump's first term.

Former Republican Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey, who considered Kyl a mentor, described the former senator in a February 2025 interview with The Associated Press as a true statesman and a "workhorse" among Washington, D.C.'s "showhorses."

Jeffries calls on Republicans to stay in Washington and work on AI safety

Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is blasting House Republicans for leaving Washington until the midterm elections rather than working to ensure the safety of artificial intelligence.

Some in the tech industry have expressed concerns that an AI unshackled from human control could be destructive — a concern President Trump has rejected as a hoax .

"The AI safety issue is very real," Jeffries said at a news conference.

To help make his point, he's noting that some industry leaders have called for the development of AI models to slow down.

"This is a serious issue. It requires serious engagement and serious and immediate action," Jeffries said. "And we're going to be here as House Democrats over the next several weeks working on this issue and other issues demanding that Republicans come back into town so we can take care of these very real concerns."

US stocks rise after oil prices fall and pressure from the bond market eases

U.S. stocks are rising Thursday and recovering most of their losses for the week.

Falling oil prices and easing pressure from the bond market helped Wall Street reverse many of its moves from the prior day , when the Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation's high inflation under control.

The S&P 500 climbed 0.9% and was on track for just its second rise in the last nine days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 213 points, or 0.4%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.4% higher.

Stocks got a boost after the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil slid 2.3% to $103.38. That's down sharply from the nearly $110 it reached earlier in the week on worries that the war with Iran will keep oil bottled up in the Middle East instead of going to customers worldwide.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has rallied 'middle powers'

Carney has repeatedly urged what he calls middle powers to resist economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, "we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered."

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's ambassador-designate to the EU, said Ottawa wants "to get as close as we possibly can" to Europe while increasing Canada's independence.

While associate membership remains to be negotiated, Canada has already taken a major step. This year, it became the first non-European country to join the EU's 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe increases defense spending.

The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and digital trade.

articles.title: Watch Mitch McConnell cast deciding vote on Senate farm bill
articles.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell, who returned to Congress in September after being hospitalized in June, cast the deciding vote to advance a Senate farm bill.
articles.body:
Sen. Mitch McConnell , R-Kentucky, cast a crucial vote for Senate Republicans to advance a farm bill on Sept. 16, days after returning to Congress from a months-long absence.

With McConnell's vote, the Senate Agriculture Committee moved to advance a farm bill , or a massive legislative package that sets national agriculture, nutrition, conservation and forestry policy , out of committee. Despite opposition from Democrats on the committee, the bill advanced 12-11 with Republicans voting along party lines.

The Republican senator returned to the Senate on Sept. 14, capping his prolonged absence after a fall and bout with pneumonia landed him in the hospital.

McConnell's time away from Capitol Hill sparked widespread speculation about his well-being.

"I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues," he said in a Sept. 14 statement before casting an early evening vote, his first since his return.

Republican leader McConnell returns to Senate post-recovery

U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 14, 2026, in Washington, DC. This is McConnell’s first public appearance in over 90 days after he recovered from a fall and illness.

Watch Mitch McConnell cast key farm bill vote

McConnell, sitting in a wheelchair, cast his vote on the farm bill on Sept. 16, voting along party lines to give the legislation the push it needed to advance out of committee.

When called on, the 84-year-old appeared to raise his finger, seemingly in favor of the bill. Sen. John Hoeven, R-North Dakota, who was sitting to McConnell's left, then leaned over and appeared to say something to him.

After McConnell's name was called a second time, the senator can be heard saying "aye" in a soft-spoken voice.

Watch the video at the top of this story.

Later, McConnell posted a statement on social media , in part saying he "was proud to vote yes" on the bill.

"My hope is the bill receives robust bipartisan support on the Senate floor and demonstrates our commitment to our Nation's farmers and rural communities," he said.

Though known colloquially as the "farm bill," the legislation is titled The Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026. A sprawling agriculture package, the farm bill is usually passed every five years, though it has not been updated since 2018.

articles.title: White House pulls stalled ICE director nominee
articles.summary: The Oklahoma state trooper had no experience leading a major law enforcement agency but was close to the Homeland Security secretary.
articles.body:
The White House on Thursday withdrew the nomination of Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement after a Republican blocked his confirmation hearing.

Schroyer's nomination stalled after Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.), a foe of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, requested that the Department of Homeland Security provide his committee with more information about its investigation into two ICE and Border Patrol agents accused of killing two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January.

Paul, who as chair controls the committee's hearing and markup agenda, did not oppose Schroyer's nomination, per Drew Carmichael, a spokesperson for the senator.

Schroyer was a surprise pick to lead ICE. He had no experience leading a major law enforcement agency, let alone an organization the size of ICE. But Schroyer has close ties with the DHS secretary. Schroyer at one point led Mullin's security detail and Mullin made Schroyer a senior adviser at DHS.

The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The nomination's withdrawal is a blow to Mullin, who has faced criticism from immigration hardliners over what they have characterized as insufficient progress in achieving mass deportations of unauthorized immigrants from the United States. Mullin had defended his pick to lead ICE, saying he wanted someone who could be confirmed in the Senate.

Mullin's pitch for putting Schroyer in the role in part involved highlighting his experience with helping stand up special units in the Oklahoma Highway Patrol to locate abducted children, as well as his work implementing a state program allowing local police departments to work with ICE on arresting undocumented immigrants.

But immigration hardliners weren't convinced. They and others in the administration doubted Schroyer could lead the complex agency — or even clear the Senate.

Schroyer's abrupt exit means the agency's streak of not having a confirmed leader at the top ranks will continue. The Senate has not confirmed an ICE director since 2014 and there is pessimism within the administration's ranks that the Senate could confirm any nominee with a significant track record at ICE, given how polarizing the agency has become under President Donald Trump.

Acting ICE chief David Venturella, a close ally of White House border czar Tom Homan, has led ICE while Schroyer's nomination was pending. Under federal law, as long as a nominee is pending Venturella can serve in that role indefinitely. Now, the clock starts ticking on a 210 day limit for his tenure, unless someone else is nominated.

Venturella would have his own challenges if he were nominated for the role, including past work for GEO Group, a major private detention company. Some in the administration have said that association would hurt his chances at confirmation to lead ICE in Schroyer's place.
