articles.title: Unearthed audio exposes stunning El-Sayed admission about his healthcare pitch
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's 2011 comments reveal his long-standing vision for Medicare-for-all and making healthcare more expensive for wealthier patients.
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged in a 2011 podcast that his healthcare vision would make costs marginally more expensive for top earners.

El-Sayed's proposed Medicare-for-all plan would expand public coverage for everyone, regardless of income, age, or job.

Critics argue that the plan is too expensive and would require income taxes to at least double to cover the massive cost of government-run care.

Over a decade before becoming the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged that his vision for healthcare would require different costs for patients depending on wealth status.

"We're actually just going to give other people access to what you have and make yours more expensive. We're not asking you to lose access. We're just making yours more expensive. And not that much so, in fact. We're making it marginally more expensive," El-Sayed said in a 2011 appearance on the "Sense and Sustainability" podcast.

His resurfaced comments, made as part of a program on inequalities in healthcare, reveal El-Sayed's long-standing thinking behind his proposed policy changes.

Fifteen years later, El-Sayed has made an expansion of healthcare in the U.S. a key part of his platform as he wages a bid to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters , D-Mich.

In particular, he has championed Medicare-for-all, an expansion of the federal program that covers healthcare costs for U.S. citizens over the age of 65 and for some younger recipients with long-term disabilities.

El-Sayed's plan would expand public coverage for everyone, regardless of income, age or job.

" Medicare-for-all means no premium, no co-pay, no deductible. Doesn't matter if you get a job, lose a job, turn 26, turn 65, get married, get divorced — it is there for you," El-Sayed said in a post to X earlier this year.

Skeptics of the plan argue it is too expensive and does little to address existing inefficiencies in the American healthcare system.

In 2019, Sen. John Barrasso , R-Wyo., took to the Senate floor to blast the idea, calling it a straitjacket solution that would undermine health care quality.

"The [Congressional Budget Office] projects in its report on a single-payer plan that government spending on health care would increase substantially. They go on to say to cover the massive cost of government-run care, income taxes would have to at least double. Income taxes, American families — at least double," Barrasso said.

"Mark my words, Medicare-for-all would soon become Medicare for none."

Despite its hefty price tag, in El-Sayed's view, the plan is key to ensuring equality of outcomes, even if individual patients are charged differently. He expounded on his design in the 2011 interview.

"We wouldn't necessarily be 'stealing from the rich to give to the poor' in the U.S. because the rich will always have the ability to pay for the care that they need," El-Sayed said.

"The argument would be that everyone's premiums would go up a little bit. But for the people who actually have premiums now, what they're losing in terms of the added costs on their health plans are more manageable to them than is the absolute lack of access to healthcare among the people that don't have it now."

El-Sayed argued that his vision would make costs only marginally more expensive for top earners.

His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether it could expand on the costs of El-Sayed's vision . Having cleared the Democratic primary in Michigan, El-Sayed will face Republican challenger Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the state's Nov. 3 general election.

articles.title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker called out by MS NOW hosts in fiery exchange over him being a drag for Democrats
articles.summary: Hasan Piker clashed with MS NOW's "Clock It" podcast hosts over his anti-Israel stance as Symone Sanders Townsend said she'd tell candidates to disavow him.
articles.body:
MS NOW hosts clashed with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker over his political influence and anti-Israel stance, with Symone Sanders Townsend warning candidates to disavow him.

Piker claimed AIPAC was behind Democrats criticizing him and maintained his view that Israel is worse than Hamas, citing the conditions brought about by the occupation.

Former Democratic operative warns that Hasan Piker, seen as the 'face of the progressive movement,' could become a campaign issue for candidates due to his controversial statements.

Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker clashed with two MS NOW hosts on Wednesday on multiple issues, including his political influence and his anti-Israel stance, as Symone Sanders Townsend told the streamer point-blank she would be telling candidates she worked for to absolutely "disavow" him.

"I used to work campaigns, Hasan, and I have to tell you, if I was a strategist or a consultant or the political director on one of these campaigns, I would absolutely be telling my people to disavow you," Sanders Townsend told Piker in an interview on her "Clock It" podcast, which she co-hosts with Eugene Daniels. "I really would, because we wanna win! We wanna win, and so, like, if you're not gonna help people win, distance."

Piker acknowledged the disagreement between them as Townsend continued, "I've elected people, though. You've never elected anybody."

Piker also maintained his view that Israel is worse than Hamas , though he acknowledged it was a provocative statement. "I do believe that," he said.

"Is Hamas a religious fundamentalist operation that have engaged in violent actions? Of course they have, absolutely," Piker continued. "But that violence is directly born out of, and even that repression is directly born out of, the conditions brought about by the occupation that's been going on for 80 plus years."

Daniels pressed the Twitch streamer on whether he understood that it sounded like he was endorsing violence by making that argument.

"Do you understand that that's how people hear it? And is that what you are endorsing?" Daniels asked.

"So this, again, goes back to the same — this goes back to the same dynamic, right?" Piker said. "Structural violence and state violence is oftentimes made to be invisible. So when Israel as a state is operating its normal state functions, and sometimes it can come across as excessive, right? It's not seen as violent."

"It's no different than when people protest against police violence and police brutality. The brutality of the police is systemic violence, and therefore it's normalized," he added.

"It's made to be invisible," Piker continued. "Whereas when people protest against the police, that is all of a sudden chaotic, that's all of a sudden violent. It's never violent when the police actually release tear gas on protesters. It's violence if the protesters use leaf blowers to blow that tear gas."

Sanders Townsend jumped in to reject the comparison to protesting the police.

"I'm gonna let Eugene move on, but I just want to note, it sounds like the example that you just gave that the people who are protesting the police are Hamas. And I just would reject that as somebody who has protested the police before, but we can move on," Sanders Townsend said.

"Symone Sanders Townsend is putting her finger on a real tension for Democrats heading into the midterms," Y. David Scharf, chair of Morrison Cohen's Government Strategies & Controversies practice, told Fox News Digital . "Hasan Piker gives candidates access to a large, young audience that traditional political media often doesn't reach. But he also gives Republicans a ready-made way to force those candidates to answer for statements they didn't make."

"Every candidate on the record defending him, appearing with him, or refusing to distance themselves from him helps turn him into a campaign issue," he added.

"In safe blue districts, that may not matter," Scharf said. "In a race as close as Michigan's Senate contest, it can. That's why Sanders Townsend, who has actually run campaigns, is looking at this very differently than Piker is. He's building an audience. She's counting votes."

Piker insisted during a Friday livestream it was his "God-given" and "constitutionally protected right" to proclaim hatred for America.

During one of his lengthy shows, Piker responded to an attack ad against Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed based on his connection to Piker and his past controversial statements claiming to "hate" America.

"Bro, I hate this country, dude. I hate America," Piker said in clips featured on the ad. "Oh God, I f---ing hate America so much."

Piker argued after showing the clip that it was "clear" that he was angry at "what America as the American government is doing to Americans and to everyone else" but nevertheless defended his right to say he hates the country.

"Of course, I'm a godd--- American. It is my godd--- God-given and constitutionally protected right to say I hate America if America is actually f---ing over Americans," he said. "You can clip chimp it all day. It doesn't change that. It doesn't change that mentality."

"To present this as like, 'Oh, these guys are real America haters,' as some liberals have been doing on the timeline, as virtually the entirety of the Republican Party is doing, is so f---ing stupid," Piker added.

articles.title: Killing endangered wildlife is legal if they aren't the target, new Trump rule says
articles.summary: Killing endangered animals while logging a forest or building a dam would not be considered illegal unless the animals were specifically targeted, under a ne...
articles.body:
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — Killing endangered animals while logging a forest or building a dam would not be considered illegal unless the animals were specifically targeted, under a new interpretation of the Endangered Species Act by President Donald Trump's administration that marks a sea change in how the landmark environmental law is enforced.

A directive sent to U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service employees this week says imperiled animals or plants must be intentionally targeted for their killing to be considered illegal.

That's a sharp turnaround from past practice at the wildlife service, which historically held people liable even for accidentally harming protected species such as grizzly bears , manatees and spotted owls .

Former Fish and Wildlife director says the change 'creates a huge loophole'

Experts said the change would allow timber companies to log forests in the Pacific Northwest even if they knew that doing so could kill imperiled birds nesting in the trees, or for developers to build a dam knowing it would kill salmon.

"This cuts against the entire history of the Endangered Species Act," said Dan Ashe, who led the Fish and Wildlife Service under former President Barack Obama.

"It just creates a huge loophole," added Ashe, who is now president of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. "It completely relieves people of any responsibility for their actions, even consequences that can be easily predicted."

Encouraged by Republican lawmakers and industry lobbyists, officials under Trump have moved to dismantle key parts of the endangered species law and make companies exempt from its regulations. Administration officials have said they are returning the law to its original intent, following a 2024 Supreme Court decision that limited the authority of federal agencies to interpret environmental statutes passed by Congress.

States and conservation groups have filed numerous lawsuits seeking to turn back the changes .

The directive follows a rule change defining 'harm' under Endangered Species Act

The new interpretation of what it means to harm — or "take" — a species was detailed in a Sept. 14 directive from Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik.

"Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them," Nesvik wrote, adding that the bats would only be impacted "indirectly and accidentally."

The directive, reported earlier by The New York Times, leans heavily on a dissenting opinion from former Justice Antonin Scalia in a 1995 Supreme Court case. It comes on the heels of a new rule from the wildlife service in July that narrowed the definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act, or ESA.

Nesvik's directive will guide how that new rule is put into action, according to a Thursday statement from the Interior Department, which includes the Fish and Wildlife Service.

"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," Interior Department officials said.

For decades, the government had defined harm to imperiled animals broadly to include encroachments on places where they live. Environmentalists warn the recent moves, if allowed to stand, will speed extinctions by letting protected species be killed and opening the door to habitat destruction .

"This is basically a free-for-all," said Noah Greenwald with the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental group. "It's a radical reinterpretation that would put polluters and other industry before the natural world."

Federal officials have long worked with companies and individuals to minimize harm to species by crafting habitat protection plans and issuing permits for some incidental killings.

Under the new interpretation of the law, the only people needing such a permit would be those acting directly against animals, such as hunters, trappers, anglers and perhaps pesticide users, said Sandi Snodgrass, an attorney with Holland and Hart in Denver whose clients include developers, energy companies and utilities.

But Snodgrass said some companies may still seek permits to guard against changes by future administrations or to protect themselves against citizen lawsuits.

The Endangered Species Act is credited with bringing back iconic animals — including the bald eagle, American alligator and California condor — from the brink of extinction.

Republicans rolled back several provisions of the law in Trump's first term, only to have those moves reversed under Democratic President Joe Biden, then revived yet again during Trump's second term.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: 71% think Trump administration lacks plan to end Iran war
articles.summary: A Fox News poll finds 70% of voters say Trump lacks a clear strategy for the Iran war, while 60% now call the military action the wrong decision.
articles.body: Nearly seven months into the war with Iran, a new Fox News national survey finds views souring as voters feel the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the war, a growing number think the conflict will make the U.S. less safe and a majority believes the decision to take military action was wrong. Seven in 10 voters think the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, including 95% of Democrats, 83% of independents and 43% of Republicans. In addition, a growing 47% of voters say the conflict will make the U.S. less safe in the long run, up from 39% in April. By comparison, 32% think it will make the country safer, and 20% say there will be no difference. The rise in concern is largest among White voters, voters under 45 and independents. Sixty percent say U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, while 37% say it was right, widening the margin to 23 points, up from 17 points in June (58% to 41%). Attitudes against the war have increased modestly across most demographic groups, with the largest shifts among Hispanic voters, voters under age 30, moderates and voters 65 and over. FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE "Typically, the public rallies around the president in response to a foreign policy crisis," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But two things are different here. First, President Trump hasn’t consistently and forcefully made the case for the war, and the U.S. doesn’t have boots on the ground. Both of those things matter for public opinion." FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Trump’s overall job performance stands at 39% approval and 61% disapproval. The president’s ratings on foreign policy are underwater by 24 points. His 37% approval is a second-term low and is just one point above his first-term low of 36% in September 2019. When asked to name the most important issue facing the country, in their own words, only 4% of voters say Iran and a miniscule 1% name foreign policy in general. By comparison, 34% mention the top issue of the cost of living. Meanwhile, by a 10-point margin, more voters say the Democrats are better equipped to handle foreign policy than the Republicans, a reversal from the previous midterm cycle when Republicans were more trusted by 6 points in September 2022. Israel and Ukraine A low of 48% say they side more with the Israelis than the Palestinians (38%) in the ongoing conflict in Gaza. That is down from 54% in June and a high of 68% at the conflict’s outset in October 2023. Since 2023, the sharpest decline in support for Israel — down at least 20 points — comes from women, Hispanic voters, voters under age 45, voters with a college degree and Democrats. Republican support has fallen 10 points during the same time. On Ukraine, voters favor the U.S. continuing to provide financial aid to fight Russia by 16 points (55% to 39%), roughly unchanged during the past two years. Democrats favor supporting Ukraine, while Republicans and independents are divided. One more thing… Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s upcoming visit to the U.S., more than twice as many voters say Trump is not tough enough on China (45%) as say he is too tough (20%). Three in 10 (30%) say his approach is about right. There is bipartisan agreement on this: the largest share of Democrats (44%), Republicans (47%), and independents (44%) say Trump is not tough enough on China. Republicans are more split, with 43% saying his approach is about right. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

articles.title: Unearthed clip exposes what 'DEI Queen' in razor-thin House race thought of 'Back the Blue' law
articles.summary: Christina Bohannan called Iowa's Back the Blue law an "overreaction" to the George Floyd riots, fueling fresh Republican soft-on-crime attacks.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Christina Bohannan, an Iowa state legislator and the Democratic nominee in one of the country’s most competitive districts, once opposed an Iowa Back the Blue law passed in the wake of the 2020 George Floyd riots, calling it an "overreaction." "I think that we’re seeing a backlash and, frankly, an exaggerated backlash, an overreaction to all of that," Bohannan said at a 2021 virtual legislative forum on social justice issues. "That’s what’s happening. A lot of this is happening because they just don’t have a lot of minorities in their districts. They don’t interact with people on any kind of regular basis, and, so, they don’t see these issues." To some onlooking critics, her resurfaced comments are further proof of what they’ve characterized as her soft-on-crime stances, positions they believe are at odds with the electorate of the Hawkeye State as she wages her third campaign to unseat Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa. WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN "Christina Bohannan achieved the ultra rare final boss level of woke where police are bad, criminals are good and anyone who disagrees is racist," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "There is a reason why this DEI queen has been rejected twice by voters. She is straight up nuts, and her soft-on-crime agenda would endanger all Iowans." Bohannan launched her career in education, teaching at the University of Iowa College of Law, where she remained until 2020, when she won a seat in the Iowa House of Representatives, unseating a 20-year Democratic incumbent. Bohannan has run for Congress before. In 2022, she lost to Miller-Meeks in a 53.4% to 46.6% contest. She tried again in 2024 and got closer, losing by a fraction of a percent, 50.0% to 49.8%, and by just 799 votes. VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP In all three races, Republicans have attacked her for her statements as an academic and her voting record as a state legislator, painting her as a soft-on-crime candidate. In the resurfaced clip, Bohannan was referring to Senate File 342, signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in 2021. Among other provisions, the bill raised penalties for rioting, making it a class D felony punishable by five years behind bars, and implemented more stringent punishments for unlawful assembly. The law came amid a wave of anti-police sentiment that swept the country after George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, died after Officer Derek Chauvin knelt on his neck area during a restraint. The incident sparked widespread debate about law enforcement safety and profiling. Where states like Minnesota and Washington passed restrictions on police and other law enforcement officers, Iowa lawmakers rallied to their support. Iowa Rep. Jarad Klein, a Republican and the bill’s sponsor, framed the legislation as a clear way to support embattled public servants in a floor speech. "Let me be clear: If you support law enforcement, truly support law enforcement, you will be voting ‘yes’ tonight. If you stand up and say you support law enforcement, your words will become meaningless with a ‘no’ vote. Actions speak louder than words," Klein said. Gov. Reynolds echoed that thinking at her signing. "I made it clear in my Condition of the State Address that Iowa’s law enforcement will always have my respect, and I will always have their back. Today’s bill embodies that commitment in a historic way. The public peace is too important, and the safety of our officers too precious to tolerate destructive behavior," Reynolds said in a press release. For her part, Bohannan said she opposed the legislation, arguing it went too far. "The bill that’s coming over to the House from the Senate about the protestors actually would make it OK for a person to drive negligently or grossly negligently and hit a protester, and there would be immunity for that. It’s sick. These are kids, mostly," she said. UNEARTHED CLIP EXPOSES MORE ANTI-POLICE RHETORIC AS EL-SAYED GETS GRILLED FOR DELETING SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS The final version of the bill does have a provision that protects drivers from civil liability. But it only applies to drivers "exercising due care" and who cause injury to someone engaging in disorderly conduct by blocking traffic on a public street or highway. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bohannan’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital on her statements from 2021 or whether she stood by her views of the Back the Blue bill.

articles.title: Trump's EPA reforms are a huge boost to manufacturers, but there's more red tape to cut: expert
articles.summary: NAM CEO Jay Timmons says Trump EPA rollback of Biden-era power plant emissions standards is a game changer but warns more permitting reform is needed.
articles.body: trump The Trump administration's move to eliminate a swath of Biden-era power plant emissions standards will be a game changer for the U.S. economy, National Association of Manufacturers CEO Jay Timmons told Fox News Digital. Timmons hailed EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for the move announced this week but noted that even more red tape remains to be cut. "It really sent a signal to manufacturers that the administration was listening to our concerns," Timmons said of the cuts to power plant emissions standards. TRUMP'S EPA CHIEF PUSHES BACK ON CLIMATE SKEPTICS BEING LABELED 'SCIENCE DENIERS' He said NAM and other groups had objected to former President Joe Biden's 2024 standards "very, very clearly" at the time, saying the standards were "simply unworkable." "The timeline that they had proposed was just, it wasn't feasible. Not that the aspirations for, you know, for cleaner air and a healthier environment aren't good aspirations," Timmons said. "I think we all share that. I know the current EPA and Administrator Zeldin certainly share those objectives, but how you get there really matters and whether manufacturers are able to meet the challenge. Timmons noted that the Biden administration had heard its concerns but simply disagreed. TRUMP-APPROVED ENERGY PROJECTS AT RISK OF SUDDEN DEATH BY NEXT HOSTILE PRESIDENT The emissions regulations cut this week were removed by executive fiat, but Timmons says more lasting change must come through Congress as manufacturers hope to avoid regulatory whiplash between administrations. "Uncertainty is the absolute worst enemy for manufacturers because manufacturers are on a very long-term horizon when it comes to planning and strategy, product development, research development. So, when administrations change, there has often been kind of that pendulum swing," Timmons said. SEN KEVIN CRAMER: CHINA BUILDS FOR WAR WHILE AMERICA WAITS ON PERMITS One area he said could use further reform is permitting. NAM polling found that 80% of manufacturers say the length and complexity of the permitting process is harmful to increasing investment. As many as 87% of manufacturers told NAM they would expand business operations, hire more workers or increase wages and benefits if the permitting process was more streamlined. SENATE MOVES TO UNSHACKLE AMERICA'S DRIVERS FROM CALIFORNIA'S 'CLIMATE ZEALOTS' Timmons said it is critical for Congress to hear directly from manufacturers when drafting legislation, however. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There needs to be more opportunities for business to be at the table. To really explain what the art of the possible is. No one is saying that we should not be working hard to achieve cleaner air, cleaner water, healthier communities. In fact, we're saying exactly that. We should be part of the solution to make that happen," he said.

articles.standfirst: Levantamento do g1 com dados do TSE mostra que 53% dos mesários registrados têm 40 anos ou mais e 58% são voluntários. Base reúne 1,84 milhão de pessoas.
articles.summary: Base do TSE reúne 1,84 milhão de mesários: 53% têm 40 anos ou mais e 58% são voluntários. Veja o perfil por gênero, idade, cor ou raça e atuação no exterior.
articles.body:
As mulheres são pouco mais de sete em cada dez mesários registrados para o primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. Elas somam 1,31 milhão de pessoas e representam 71,4% do total, segundo levantamento do g1 com dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). A participação feminina na função supera a observada em 2022, de 68,3%, e em 2018, de 66,4%.

👀A composição por idade também mudou: pessoas com 40 anos ou mais passaram a ser maioria nos registros deste ano (53%), enquanto aquelas com idade entre 18 e 29 anos perderam espaço e representam 18,2% do total. Além disso, mais da metade dos mesários (58%) se apresentou de forma voluntária para a função.

O levantamento considera 1.837.846 mesários registrados no Brasil e no exterior na base atualizada em 17 de setembro. Como os dados foram extraídos antes da votação, os números retratam os registros disponíveis nessa data, e não o comparecimento efetivo no dia da eleição.

Cabe a esses eleitores organizar o trabalho nas seções, conferir a identidade de quem vai votar e registrar as ocorrências da votação. Cada mesa receptora de votos tem quatro integrantes: presidente, primeiro mesário, segundo mesário e secretário.

🔎 O que cada um faz, segundo o TSE: o presidente coordena os trabalhos, inicia e encerra a votação e autoriza os eleitores a votar. Os demais integrantes conferem a identidade de quem comparece à seção, organizam a fila respeitando as prioridades de atendimento, entregam os comprovantes de votação e registram em ata as ocorrências do dia.

Total de mesários registrados: 1.837.846;

Pessoas com 40 anos ou mais : 974.102, ou 53%;

Pessoas de 18 a 29 anos : 333.760, ou 18,2%;

Há 21 registros sem informação de gênero.

Mudança no perfil dos mesários desde as eleições 2018 até 2026 — Foto: Arte g1

Confira os números completos no gráfico ao final do texto.

Mulheres são maioria em todos os estados

Mesário conferem dados dos eleitores — Foto: Érika Rios

A presença feminina predomina nos 26 estados e no Distrito Federal. O Espírito Santo tem a maior proporção de mulheres entre os mesários registrados: 76,3%. Na sequência aparecem Mato Grosso, com 75,5%, Tocantins, com 75,1%, e Minas Gerais, com 74,8%.

Mesmo nos estados com as menores proporções, elas representam mais de seis em cada dez mesários. É o caso da Paraíba, com 63,3%, do Rio Grande do Norte, com 64,2%, e de Alagoas, com 64,7%.

Na comparação entre as três eleições, a participação das mulheres aumentou:

2026 : 71,4%, com 1.311.506 registradas até 17 de setembro.

O avanço foi de 3,1 pontos percentuais em relação a 2022.

Justiça Eleitoral procura brasileiros para o serviço de mesário — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A mudança etária aparece tanto na faixa mais frequente quanto na distribuição do conjunto dos mesários.

Em 2018, o maior grupo tinha de 30 a 34 anos. Em 2022, a faixa predominante passou a ser a de 35 a 39 anos. Neste ano, são os mesários de 40 a 44 anos, que somam 323.076 pessoas, ou 17,6% do total.

Considerando todas as faixas a partir dos 40 anos, a participação passou de 32,2% em 2018 para 40,4% em 2022 e chegou a 53% nos registros de 2026.

No sentido contrário, os jovens de 18 a 29 anos representavam 33,6% em 2018 e 27,3% em 2022. Agora, são 18,2%. A diferença em relação à eleição anterior é de 9,1 pontos percentuais.

De 18 a 29 anos: 333.760 pessoas, ou 18,2%;

De Santa Maria, Wanderson Thomaz, engenheiro agrônomo, se oferece para ser mesário em todas as eleições — Foto: Juliana Motta/RBS TV

Dos mesários registrados para este ano, 1.066.360 são classificados como voluntários, o equivalente a 58%. Os outros 771.486, ou 42%, estão na categoria de não voluntários.

Ser voluntário significa se colocar à disposição da Justiça Eleitoral. A inscrição, porém, não garante a atuação: o cartório verifica a existência de vagas e de impedimentos antes de fazer a convocação. Segundo o TSE, a escolha dá preferência a eleitores do próprio local de votação, com prioridade para voluntários.

🤔 Como funciona a seleção : o cartório eleitoral verifica a existência de vagas e se o eleitor atende aos requisitos para exercer a função. Podem ser convocadas pessoas a partir dos 18 anos, em situação regular com a Justiça Eleitoral e sem impedimentos legais, mesmo que não tenham se inscrito como voluntárias. A convocação informa a função, o local e a data de trabalho, além das orientações para o treinamento.

As mulheres também são maioria entre quem se voluntariou: são 753.339.

No exterior, voluntários são menos de um quarto

Eleições 2024 em Campinas: mesário acompanha votação — Foto: Pedro Amatuzzi/g1

Nos locais de votação fora do Brasil, a base reúne 4.828 mesários , ante 3.991 em 2022. São 837 registros a mais, um crescimento de 21%. Em 2018, eram 2.966.

As mulheres também predominam nesse grupo, mas em proporção menor que no conjunto dos mesários: são 2.957, ou 61,2%.

A principal diferença está no tipo de convocação. Enquanto os voluntários representam 58,1% dos mesários que atuarão no Brasil, no exterior eles são 22,3%. Os demais 77,7% estão classificados como não voluntários.

Quem tem domicílio eleitoral no exterior vota apenas para presidente e vice-presidente. A organização da eleição fora do país cabe ao Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Distrito Federal, com apoio de consulados e missões diplomáticas.

Quase 80% não têm informação de cor ou raça

No perfil racial, 1.465.558 registros, ou 79,7% do total, aparecem sem informação de cor ou raça.

Entre os 372.288 registros que têm essa informação preenchida, a distribuição é:

Pretos e pardos, somados, representam 56,8% do grupo com informação racial disponível. Esse percentual não pode ser estendido ao conjunto dos mesários, porque não se conhece o perfil dos registros sem preenchimento.

Nos arquivos de 2018 e 2022 analisados, todos os registros aparecem como “não informado” nesse campo.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: Proporção de candidatos milionários cresce no país | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidenciáveis concentram a maior proporção de candidatos milionários, enquanto as disputas para deputado têm as maiores parcelas de concorrentes sem bens declarados. Entre os partidos, PRTB, PSD e PP registram os maiores percentuais de candidatos com patrimônio declarado de pelo menos R$ 1 milhão.
articles.summary: Levantamento aponta que candidatos milionários nas eleições 2026 já somam 30% do total, com maior concentração de riqueza na disputa pela Presidência.
articles.body:
Os milionários ganharam espaço entre os candidatos nas eleições de 2026. Dos concorrentes deste ano, 6.354 declararam patrimônio de pelo menos R$ 1 milhão, o equivalente a 30,3% do total. Outros 7.078 (33,8%) não informaram bens.

A presença dos candidatos milionários é maior nas disputas pelos cargos nacionais e majoritários. Já entre os concorrentes a deputado, cresce a fatia daqueles sem patrimônio declarado. A composição varia também conforme a unidade da Federação e o partido.

🔍 Os dados são das declarações de bens apresentadas pelos próprios candidatos à Justiça Eleitoral. O levantamento considera milionário quem declarou patrimônio total de pelo menos R$ 1 milhão. Na categoria sem patrimônio estão tanto os candidatos que declararam valor total igual a zero quanto aqueles sem registro de bens na base consultada.

O perfil patrimonial dos candidatos mudou desde a eleição de 2022. Em 2026, aumentou a proporção de concorrentes milionários, enquanto caiu a daqueles sem patrimônio declarado.

Perfil patrimonial dos candidatos muda nas eleições de 2026 — Foto: Arte/g1

Nas eleições de 2026, mais de 6 mil candidatos declararam patrimônio de pelo menos R$ 1 milhão.

A maior concentração de milionários está entre os candidatos a presidente e vice-presidente. Nos dois cargos, 69% dos concorrentes declararam patrimônio de pelo menos R$ 1 milhão, 23% estão na faixa intermediária e 8% não declararam bens.

É também nessas duas disputas que o contraste entre os extremos é mais acentuado: a parcela de milionários supera em 61 pontos percentuais a de candidatos sem patrimônio declarado.

Como se distribui o patrimônio dos candidatos em 2026 — Foto: Arte/g1

Para deputado estadual, a relação se inverte: os candidatos sem patrimônio são 8 pontos percentuais mais numerosos proporcionalmente do que os milionários.

A tendência também aparece nas demais disputas legislativas, que concentram parcela maior de candidatos sem bens declarados do que os cargos majoritários.

Entre os partidos, as maiores proporções de milionários estão no PRTB, PSD e PP, com 58%, 50% e 49% das candidaturas com mais de R$ 1 milhão declarados.

No outro extremo, os partidos com maiores proporções de candidatos sem patrimônio declarado são PCO (75%), DC (63%) e Democrata (63%).

Perfil patrimonial dos candidatos, por partido — Foto: Arte/g1

O g1 analisou os dados de candidaturas e de bens declarados ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) nas eleições de 2022 e 2026 (dados extraídos no dia 14 de agosto). O patrimônio de cada candidato foi calculado pela soma dos bens informados à Justiça Eleitoral.

Foram considerados milionários os candidatos com patrimônio declarado de pelo menos R$ 1 milhão e classificados como de patrimônio zero aqueles que não declararam bens. A partir desses dados, o foi possível comparar a participação desses grupos no total de candidaturas e por cargo, estado e partido.

articles.title: ‘É de direita ou esquerda?’: buscas sobre espectro político de candidatos disparam; especialistas analisam impacto | G1
articles.standfirst: As dúvidas sobre a inclinação ideológica de candidatos, partidos políticos e figuras públicas estiveram entre os principais interesses dos usuários desde o início da campanha.
articles.summary: As dúvidas sobre a inclinação ideológica de candidatos, partidos políticos e figuras públicas estiveram entre os principais interesses dos usuários desde o início da campanha.
articles.body:
A três semanas do primeiro turno das Eleições de 2026 , as buscas no Google por nomes de candidatos acompanhadas pela pergunta “é de direita ou esquerda?” quase triplicaram no Brasil desde o início da campanha eleitoral , em 16 de agosto. Os dados foram compilados pela empresa.

As dúvidas sobre a inclinação ideológica de candidatos, partidos políticos e figuras públicas estiveram entre os principais interesses dos usuários. ( Veja os mais buscados nos últimos sete dias )

🔎 O primeiro turno das Eleições 2026 está previsto para 4 de outubro. Em caso de segundo turno, a votação para os cargos do Executivo ocorrerá em 25 de outubro.

Para o cientista político Elias Tavares, as eleições deste ano são marcadas pela busca por identidade política, e os termos “direita” e “esquerda” funcionam como um filtro inicial para o eleitor.

“O eleitor tenta descobrir se existe um ‘match’ entre aquele candidato e aquilo em que ele mesmo acredita. Em muitos casos, a primeira pergunta já não é necessariamente ‘o que esse candidato propõe?’, mas, sim, ‘ele está de qual lado?’. Direita e esquerda ajudam o eleitor a antecipar posições, alianças e valores”, afirmou.

O cientista político Samuel Oliveira afirma que, em um cenário de polarização, essa preocupação em identificar políticos como de direita ou de esquerda pode alcançar também as disputas para deputado e senador, e não apenas a eleição presidencial.

Para ele, os dados não necessariamente indicam um eleitor mais ideológico, mas podem apontar para um eleitor mais desconfiado.

“Ele quer saber primeiro de que lado o candidato está, para depois decidir se vale a pena ouvi-lo. A polarização, então, deixa de ser apenas uma preferência e passa a funcionar como filtro”, disse.

O interesse por definições ideológicas também apareceu nas buscas relacionadas aos cargos em disputa. Nos últimos 30 dias, as pesquisas pelos termos "deputado esquerda" e "deputado direita" cresceram 600% e 1.200%, respectivamente, no Brasil.

articles.title: Entenda se o governo pode reajustar benefício social em ano eleitoral e diferenças de aumentos de Lula e Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Reajuste de 15,04% por Lula reacendeu o debate sobre mudanças em benefícios sociais antes das eleições, como ocorreu com a "PEC Kamicaze", aprovada em 2022 pelo Congresso do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).
articles.summary: Reajuste de 15,04% por Lula reacendeu o debate sobre mudanças em benefícios sociais antes das eleições, como ocorreu com a "PEC Kamicaze", aprovada em 2022 pelo Congresso do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).
articles.body:
Especialistas entendem que o reajuste de 15,04% no valor do Bolsa Família concedido pelo governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) apenas repõe a inflação e não é proibido pela legislação eleitoral. Eles questionam, no entanto, o momento escolhido para o anúncio e alertam para possíveis impactos sobre as contas públicas, a inflação e os juros nos próximos anos. ( Veja mais detalhes )

O reajuste reacendeu o debate sobre mudanças em benefícios sociais a poucas semanas das eleições, como ocorreu com a "PEC Kamicaze", aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional com o apoio do governo do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), em 2022.

Há, entretanto, diferenças entre a situação de 2022 e a mudança anunciada agora pelo governo Lula. O valor do Auxílio Brasil (atual Bolsa Família) foi reajustado em 50%, passando de R$ 400 para R$ 600. À época, também houve a elevação do Auxílio-Gás para o valor de um botijão e a criação de um novo benefício: um "voucher" de R$ 1 mil para caminhoneiros.

Em 2024, o STF declarou inconstitucionais dispositivos da PEC , que criava um “estado de emergência” que permitiu a ampliação de benefícios sociais. Os ministros disseram que, para manter a paridade de armas e a liberdade de voto, é preciso impedir a utilização da máquina pública para influenciar a decisão do eleitorado a favor ou contra qualquer candidato.

“A indevida utilização da máquina pública como meio para obtenção de vantagens eleitorais, de modo geral, caracteriza o abuso de uma circunstância fática de proeminência e, por conseguinte, evidencia ofensa ao núcleo essencial da liberdade de voto e paridade de armas, tendo em vista o emprego abusivo, arbitrário e injustificado de instrumentos que acentuam o desequilíbrio entre os candidatos”, diz a decisão do STF.

De acordo com o governo Lula, a atualização dos valores somente corrigiu a variação acumulada do Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor (INPC), entre março de 2023 e agosto de 2026, sem ganho real. ( Veja o que o governo diz sobre o reajuste )

A Lei das Eleições, de 1997, que dispõe sobre as regras para a disputa eleitoral, proíbe a distribuição gratuita de bens, valores ou benefícios em ano de eleição, com exceções. Estão neste rol os programas autorizados em lei e que já tenham passado por execução orçamentária no ano anterior, como o Bolsa Família.

Não há, em geral, um precedente do TSE dizendo literalmente que "é permitida a correção do benefício pela inflação". A analogia mais clara aparece na jurisprudência sobre remuneração de servidores. O TSE entende que a proibição eleitoral recai sobre aumentos reais, mas não sobre a recomposição inflacionária do poder aquisitivo.

“É uma interpretação baseada nas chamadas condutas vedadas do artigo 73 da lei das eleições, com a jurisprudência do TSE”, explica o advogado eleitoral e membro da Academia Brasileira de Direito Eleitoral e Político (Abradep) Alexandre Bissoli.

O entendimento é que a mera atualização monetária para preservar o valor real de um programa já existente não se confunde com a criação ou ampliação eleitoreira de benefício. ( Veja mais detalhes sobre a discussão abaixo )

No caso do Bolsa Família, a lei que recriou o programa em 2023 permite ao governo corrigir os valores e proíbe a redução do benefício.

O deputado federal e candidato à reeleição Zé Tovão (PL-SC), aliado do senador e candidato à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), acionou o TSE pedindo a suspensão do reajuste. O ministro André Mendonça foi sorteado relator do caso e negou o pedido de suspensão, sem apreciar o mérito, alegando que o pedido não poderia ser feito por um candidato a deputado federal.

No julgamento no STF, prevaleceu a divergência aberta pelo decano do STF, ministro Gilmar Mendes. O ministro considerou que, mesmo que as medidas aprovadas naquela época já tivessem sido realizadas, o caso ainda deveria ser discutido pela Corte.

Acompanharam este posicionamento os ministros:

Mendes apontou, no voto, a preocupação com uma eventual repetição de situações como esta. Ressaltou que os benefícios foram concedidos em meio ao processo eleitoral.

"Que possamos sinalizar que valeu uma vez, e não mais. Porque se não nós corremos o risco de aprimoramento desse modelo", afirmou.

"É de extrema relevância um pronunciamento dessa Corte sobre essa matéria. Sob pena de, em situações que venham a surgir no futuro, que tenhamos sempre um bypass (desvio) da regra da anterioridade eleitoral e da violação da igualdade eleitoral", completou.

Relator do caso, o ministro André Mendonça considerou que parte dos argumentos apresentados no processo havia perdido o objeto, porque a ampliação de benefícios já havia sido implantada. Também concluiu que não houve irregularidades na tramitação da proposta. Dessa forma, votou pela rejeição da ação.

O ministro Nunes Marques votou para negar os pedidos, mantendo a validade da emenda. O ministro Cristiano Zanin não votou – está impedido por ter atuado como advogado no caso.

A jurisprudência mais clara do TSE sobre o assunto aborda o pagamento de benefícios sociais em ano de eleições.

Sobre este ponto, o TSE fixou, em uma ação de relatoria do ministro Gilmar Mendes, que é permitido o pagamento de benefícios sociais em ano eleitoral somente se houver lei de criação do programa social e da previsão e existência de execução orçamentária específica.

A Lei das Eleições diz que só podem ser mantidos em ano de eleições programas sociais autorizados em lei e já em execução orçamentária no exercício anterior, “casos em que o Ministério Público poderá promover o acompanhamento de sua execução financeira e administrativa”.

Especialistas ouvidos pelo g1/TV Globo seguem a mesma linha. Eles argumentam que existe uma proibição sobre aumento no benefício, ou seja, ganho real no valor, mas não reposição inflacionária, desde que prevista na Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA).

A Lei de Responsabilidade Fiscal (LRF) proíbe o presidente de criar novas despesas com pessoal nos 180 dias antes do término do mandato, mas essa vedação não se estende à reposição inflacionária de benefícios e não trata de eleições.

O problema estaria em reajustar acima da inflação, fora dos índices oficiais, e sem previsão orçamentária.

O Ministério da Fazenda informou que o reajuste do Bolsa Família apenas repõe as perdas inflacionárias dos últimos anos, o que não equivaleria a um aumento do benefício social. A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) afirmou que o movimento do governo segue a lei que instituiu o programa.

"Ao editar o ato, o Governo Federal exerce, portanto, a competência que o Congresso Nacional lhe atribuiu", disse o orgão.

Segundo a AGU, a correção do benefício pela inflação, sem a ampliação do público beneficiado, está "fora do alcance de qualquer vedação eleitoral".

A equipe econômica do governo negou que o reajuste tenha relação com as eleições presidenciais. O anúncio ocorre a 17 dias do primeiro turno, marcado para 4 de outubro. Lula é candidato à reeleição e tem visto, nas pesquisas mais recentes, o avanço de seu principal adversário, senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ).

"Creio que não [tem relação com as eleições]. Ficou claro que foi feito pelo esforço de cadastro. Precisávamos da clareza que temos espaço fiscal disponível. Identificamos e viemos dar a tranquilidade para o presidente que tínhamos capacidade [de reajustar]", disse o ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti.

“A primeira coisa é que não podemos deixar de considerar que faz tempo que não há reajuste. O problema é que isso está sendo feito às vésperas das eleições, então fica difícil não interpretar o movimento como eleitoreiro”, diz o economista-chefe da Análise Econômica, André Galhardo.

A equipe econômica nega que a decisão tenha motivação eleitoral. “O reajuste, em si, é justo. O problema é o momento”, avalia o professor de economia da Universidade de Brasília (UnB), José Luis Oreiro. Ele destaca, no entanto, que essa movimentação não é novidade.

“Em 2022, na campanha, aconteceu o mesmo. Isso revela uma deterioração das instituições brasileiras, com decisões que deveriam ser técnicas e automáticas virando instrumento de calendário eleitoral”, completa.

O Ministério Público junto ao Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) pediu que a Corte suspenda o reajuste anunciado pelo governo. A representação foi assinada pelo procurador Lucas Furtado.

"O decreto produz efeitos financeiros a partir do primeiro dia do mês subsequente ao de sua publicação, gerando impacto orçamentário imediato e de grande monta, sem que haja qualquer indicação de prévia dotação orçamentária ou estimativa de impacto financeiro", diz trecho do documento.

articles.title: VÍDEO: o que é e como denunciar assédio eleitoral | G1
articles.standfirst: Prática é considerada crime, e denúncias podem ser feitas ao Ministério Público do Trabalho. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Prática é considerada crime, e denúncias podem ser feitas ao Ministério Público do Trabalho. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.body:

O assédio eleitoral pode partir de chefes, mas também ocorrer entre colegas de trabalho, de forma explícita ou indireta. Entenda no vídeo acima.

articles.title: Trump administration memo reduces ESA protections
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump administration memo reduces ESA protections The Trump administration has further reduced protections for wildlife and plants under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). © Joy Asico, Associated Press Content Services for Center for Biological Diversity The law prohibits any “take” of endangered species — meaning…
articles.body:
Trump administration memo reduces ESA protections

The Trump administration has further reduced protections for wildlife and plants under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

© Joy Asico, Associated Press Content Services for Center for Biological Diversity

The law prohibits any “take” of endangered species — meaning to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect” fish, wildlife or plants classified as threatened or endangered. It also bans attempts to do so.

The administration recently repealed a previous definition of prohibited “harm” under the law, now saying that only intentional acts of “taking” a species are outlawed.

An internal memo from the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) sent out Sept. 14 states, “The Harm Rule rescinded the Services’ regulatory definitions of ‘harm’ … and adopted Justice [Antonin] Scalia’s interpretation of ‘take’ set out in the dissent in Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon.”

“Under Justice Scalia’s interpretation, ‘take’ reaches only an affirmative act that is intentionally and purposefully directed at a particular animal,” the memo continued.

According to the administration, a ship that “inadvertently” strikes a whale “has not taken it.” Another example given stated that felling a tree is not a “take” of the bats residing in it, unless the tree was specifically cut down to kill or capture them.

The internal memo was obtained and made public by the Center for Biological Diversity.

“Fish and Wildlife is going to effectively, I think, be entirely muzzled by this memo,” said Brett Hartl, the group’s government affairs director.

articles.title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has lobbied the US for years to buy F35s, the world's most advanced fighter jet.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress.

Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection.

Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access.

Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons.

Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.

He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".

Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.

They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.

The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".

It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".

"The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added.

Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.

The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".

The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.

This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.

However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May that it would procure another F-35 squadron.

This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post .

Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.

Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.

Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.

The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.

The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.

The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.

But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.

articles.title: Trump signs orders loosening hunting restrictions, teases Outdoors Act ‘2.0’
articles.summary: President Trump hosted over 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor industry officials for a dinner in the Rose Garden Thursday to announce executive orders rolling back certain hunting and fishing restrictions. “We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public, and hunters, fishers, and outdoorsmen should be able to access them,”…
articles.body:
President Trump hosted over 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor industry officials for a dinner in the Rose Garden Thursday to announce executive orders rolling back certain hunting and fishing restrictions.

“We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public, and hunters, fishers, and outdoorsmen should be able to access them,” Trump said.

One order mandates that Interior Secretary Doug Burgum expand the amount of federal land available to hunters and fishers, which builds on the administration’s order August that opened up more than 92 million acres of federal land across 32 states. Burgum attended the dinner but did not deliver remarks.

Trump also touted that his latest order rolled back Biden-era prohibiting the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle.

“Lead ammunition was a problem, huh? Is it better than other ammunition? I assume, huh? That’s pretty good,” he said. “I don’t know what the hell that means, but I know one thing: you wanted it. You wanted it, and I’m here for you.”

The second order modernizes federal fishery management and loosens restrictions on American boaters and anglers — expands fishing seasons and quotas.

The president also reflected on his 2020 Great American Outdoors Act, which provided billions of dollars to address a maintenance backlog at national parks and provided millions for the Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF).

He said a “2.0” of that legislation would be coming in the “very near future.”

articles.title: Man who sprayed Minnesota Rep. Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison
articles.summary: Anthony Kazmierczak, 56, was also sentenced to three years of supervised release in the January attack, which includes no contact with Omar.
articles.body: MINNEAPOLIS — The man who sprayed vinegar at Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors. The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan. 27 assault. At the time, Minneapolis-St. Paul was facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal officers. Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact with Omar. U.S. marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced. “This wasn’t a spur-of-the-moment act,” U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance. “An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society,” Ericksen said. Spraying anything at an elected official “is a terrifying thing, and you knew that when you did it.” Omar’s attacker apologizes for what he did Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen. He spoke about being a good neighbor, and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened. “I’ve spent enough time in jail thinking,” Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. “I really apologize to her for having put her through that,” he said, referring to Omar. In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only “it’s fuzzy” when Ericksen asked what he remembered. “I’m sorry if I scared you,” he wrote to Omar after the attack. Prosecutors cite evidence of advance planning During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spray liquid from a syringe at Omar and say she was “splitting Minnesota apart.” Omar’s security officers tackled him and turned him over to police, who arrested him. Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest. Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a U.S. officer. The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar “but would not answer their questions about his intent.” He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and to ask for bail bond company contact information. The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had “a history of mental and emotional health concerns” and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson’s disease diagnosis. Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target of President Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant rhetoric. In 2019, after Omar’s election to Congress, Trump said she should “go back” to her country of birth. He has described her as “garbage” and said she should be investigated. In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticized former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as “angry and liars.” He wrote that Trump wants the U.S. to be “stronger and more prosperous.” His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters.

articles.title: Urgent motion filed to stop carving of Trump’s name into US Institute of Peace building
articles.summary: Ousted board members say a contractor has already been selected for the project.
articles.body:
Ousted board members of the U.S. Institute of Peace are asking a federal court to block the imminent carving of President Donald Trump's name on the headquarters of the nonpartisan institution he sought to dismantle shortly after taking office.

Members of the board who were removed by the administration filed an emergency motion Thursday in Washington in a dispute that has echoes of Trump's effort to place his name on the Kennedy Center.

The motion was filed as an emergency petition, alleging that a contractor has already been selected to carve Trump's name into the Constitution Avenue headquarters that the administration sought to shutter as part of the Elon Musk-led DOGE effort to shrink the government.

The former board members said in their motion that they had asked Kenneth Jackson, the DOGE official serving as acting president of the USIP, to ensure the carving would not happen as they pursue litigation to preserve the independent nonprofit created by Congress.

"The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be 'symbolic of USIP's' independent 'mission,'" the emergency motion said. "Alteration of the design to impose a different message would cause irreparable harm."

The USIP was created under President Ronald Reagan to provide research and training aimed at promoting democracy around the world. Trump's name was added to the exterior of the building in December, shortly before the president hosted a signing ceremony at the institute with the presidents of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The bolted-on affixture is removable, and is featured next to the institute's name, which is engraved into the facade.

The institute has been locked in a legal battle with the Trump administration as it hopes to reinstate its former president ousted by Trump last year . In May 2025, a federal judge ruled that the administration's actions to dismantle the nonprofit was "unlawful" but the ruling was stayed by a federal appeals court panel a month later.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The USIP's emergency motion comes days after Trump announced the Kennedy Center would be closing following a court ruling that blocked his name from being added to the building. Trump has threatened to tear down the center, and was seen on Wednesday viewing a large printout that appeared to say "Kennedy Center DEMOLISH." The Kennedy Center, which USIP referred to in its motion, is seen as a bellwether for other institutions that Trump has sought to rebrand in his image.

"Notwithstanding the importance that the President and his supporters place on attaching his name to notable buildings," the motion said, "Appellants will suffer no harm or prejudice whatsoever if they are precluded from carving the President's name into the USIP building unless and until this litigation concludes in their favor."

articles.title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
articles.summary: The White House removed Larsson's Midnight Sun from one of its reels after the artist called the clip "dehumanising".
articles.body:
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.

The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.

The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".

In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.

Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.

In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".

Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people."

"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".

"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.

Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.

White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.

Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".

Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

articles.title: White House withdraws Lance Schroyer’s nomination to lead ICE
articles.summary: The ex-Oklahoma state trooper’s nomination had stalled in the Senate as ICE faced growing scrutiny over its operations.
articles.body:
The White House has withdrawn the nomination of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), without giving a reason for the decision.

The withdrawal was announced on Thursday. Schroyer, a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, was nominated by President Donald Trump in June but had yet to receive a hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who chairs the committee, had refused to hold a hearing until the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) provided information he had requested about civilian deaths during ICE enforcement operations .

“I don’t have a concern with who the nominee was. I had asked them to give me an update on the internal investigation into civilian deaths,” Paul told The Associated Press news agency.

Paul said he had intended to hold a hearing on Schroyer’s nomination but learned that it had been withdrawn when the White House made the decision public.

Schroyer had little experience in immigration and had not previously worked at ICE or led a major law enforcement agency. Two US officials told the Reuters news agency when he was nominated that he had been a surprise choice for the position.

When announcing Schroyer’s nomination in June, Trump said on Truth Social that he had “firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets” and called on the Senate to confirm him “IMMEDIATELY”.

The withdrawal comes as ICE remains under scrutiny over its enforcement operations as the Trump administration carries out its immigration crackdown.

Critics have raised questions about how the agency has recruited and trained officers as it rapidly expanded its workforce. Federal immigration officers have also shot and killed multiple people during enforcement operations, including two US citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.

ICE arrests have continued to increase, reaching nearly 51,000 in August, the highest monthly total of Trump’s second administration.

ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed director since 2017. David Venturella is serving as acting director after Todd Lyons resigned earlier this year.

The White House has not indicated when it might announce another nominee to lead the agency.

articles.title: Tillis supports Hegseth impeachment resolution: ‘He needs to go’

Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is renewing his call for President Trump to fire the Pentagon chief after Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned. “He needs to go, whether it’s impeachment or the most expedient route — just the president to replace him — would be great,” Tillis told…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is renewing his call for President Trump to fire the Pentagon chief after Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned.

“He needs to go, whether it’s impeachment or the most expedient route — just the president to replace him — would be great,” Tillis told reporters Thursday.

Driscoll, who resigned at the end of August, clashed with Hegseth over firings of the Army’s senior leadership and other changes to the department.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday, citing his handling of the Iran war and accusing him of violating his “oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States.”

“I’ll let the House do what the House is gonna do,” Tillis told reporters when asked whether Republicans should support the articles of impeachment. “I think I’m pretty well staked out on my assessment of Mr. Hegseth.”

Tillis, who is not seeking reelection in November, has been one of Hegseth’s most vocal Republican critics in the Senate.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” the outgoing North Carolina Republican wrote on the social platform X earlier this month.

He also accused Hegseth of pushing out experienced military officials and said the Pentagon needed a leader who would “retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” he said.

Tillis told Politico earlier this year that Trump firing Hegseth was on “a Christmas wish list,” and believed the Pentagon chief misled Trump on the dynamics of a war in Iran.

articles.title: Gen Z believes in the billionaire tax
articles.summary: More than two-thirds of Generation Z thinks wealthy Americans should pay up. A new CBS/YouGov poll released Sunday found that 69 percent of respondents under 30 favor candidates who support raising taxes on wealthy Americans. That’s a higher rate than among millennials, Gen Xers and baby boomers, though majorities in older age categories also back…
articles.body:
More than two-thirds of Generation Z thinks wealthy Americans should pay up.

A new CBS/YouGov poll released Sunday found that 69 percent of respondents under 30 favor candidates who support raising taxes on wealthy Americans.

That’s a higher rate than among millennials, Gen Xers and baby boomers, though majorities in older age categories also back higher taxes on the wealthy.

In comparison, 59 percent of respondents aged 30 to 44 and 55 percent of Americans aged 45 and older said the same.

The new polling also found that Gen Z participants were least likely to say a candidate’s stance on taxing the wealthy was irrelevant. Only 12 percent of respondents under 30 said it “would not matter either way,” lower than Americans aged 30 to 44 (19 percent), 45 to 64 (21 percent) and 65 plus (22 percent).

That suggests a number of Gen Z voters want candidates to back taxing the wealthy.

William Gale, the Arjay and Frances Fearing Miller chair in federal economic policy at the Brookings Institution, told The Hill there are some obvious reasons why such taxes might appeal to Gen Z.

He noted that Gen Z was “hit by COVID and the global financial crisis and the student loans and housing shortages,” challenges he sees as fueling a wish for a tax system that hits the wealthy harder.

The results arrive ahead of midterm elections in November when the House and Senate majorities are in play and tax issues are at the center of the discussion.

Polling on California’s Proposition 40, which would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of the state’s 200 billionaires , shows voters split nearly down the middle.

But Gen Z is not so divided. One survey found that 75 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 plan to vote in favor of the initiative.

“I think the idea of taxing the rich has a lot of support in the abstract, as you’re seeing in these surveys. It’s a different thing, though, to get a legislature to pass a specific tax increase on the wealthy,” Gale later added.

California will make its decision in November.

The CBS/YouGov poll ran Sept. 8-11, surveyed 2,460 American adults and had a 2.3 margin of sampling error.

Prove it: Gen Z wants politicians to meet them where they are

Each election young adults have voted in has been labeled as the most important of their lives, yet polls show they feel nothing is changing between each election cylcle.

Only 21 percent of young people think the American Dream is achievable, compared with 50 percent a decade ago, Fortune reports .

“The big political causes our politicians told us, Democrats and Republicans, to see did not come into fruition in ways that have tangibly changed young people’s lives,” Alex Edgar, founder of AWE Strategies, a consulting firm focused on engaging young people, told The Hill.

Cost of living and inflation are ranked as the top issue among Gen Zers, and their lack of faith in the American Dream means young adults feel frustrated with how politicians have handled affordability.

“There is a pace of change in the economy that is not reflected in political leadership,” Edgar said. This is what makes Gen Zers feel different than their older counterparts.

Jaylin Drewry, the national lead of historically Black colleges and universities at the Fair Elections Campus Vote Project, told The Hill that Gen Z feels “skeptical” about the political process.

“Gen Z has been told it’s important to participate in the voting process, and each year, they see that access to voting is being rolled back in different ways,” he added, pointing to restrictions in mail-in voting and redistricting as pain points.

There is a noticeable shift in the politics young adults grew up around to the political system they’re beginning to inherit.

Kala Washington of the Fair Elections Center told The Hill that she felt there was a “different political energy” when former President Obama was in office and that things today seem more “life or death.”

Gen Z feels optimism toward politicians who meet constituents where they are, practice what they preach, make themselves known outside of election cycles and keep their promises, Edgar, Drewry and Washington concurred.

For Edgar and Washington, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) embodies these qualities. For Drewry, Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) does. But the figures aren’t just on the left.

“The conservative movement invests a fair amount into young leaders,” Edgar said, citing the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk. “We see the impact in the number of young people with official positions in the administration.”

As the country approaches 2028, politicians have a lot of work to prove to Gen Z that they care.

“There is an opening for candidates on both sides of the aisle to come out with not just a hopeful vision for what a good life looks like for young Americans, but also policy proposals that are reflective of the unique crises young Americans are experiencing with plans on how they’re going to follow through with that,” Edgar said.

Sandwich chain Jersey Mike’s, a company valued at roughly $7.5 billion with more than 3,300 store locations, is having trouble winning over Generation Z, according to a recent Wall Street Journal article .

The Journal says the sub shop is lacking in the viral food and wellness trend departments. In other words, the fast casual chain is not fast enough, and it’s way too casual.

Seventy percent of Jersey Mike’s customers are from Generation X, while Gen Zers only make up 2 percent of the chain’s consumers (me included).

The sandwich franchise falls behind in marketing and only puts 1 percent of its spending on social media advertising. Other sub shop chains including Jimmy John’s, Firehouse Subs and Subway all spend 10 percent to 18 percent on social media campaigns.

Jersey Mike’s has tapped into former New York Giants quarterback Eli Manning and actor/comedian Danny DeVito for ads, but it sounds like they need a little more pizzazz to win over Gen Z.

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.
