articles.title: Senate Republicans rebuff Trump’s attacks on Supreme Court, Federal Reserve
articles.summary: Republican senators are siding with conservative members of the Supreme Court who came under withering attack from President Trump this week after ruling against Trump’s plan to have the U.S. Postal Service screen mail-in ballots to guard against non-citizens voting. Republican senators say the Supreme Court made the right decision to reject the plan to…
articles.body:
Republican senators are siding with conservative members of the Supreme Court who came under withering attack from President Trump this week after ruling against Trump’s plan to have the U.S. Postal Service screen mail-in ballots to guard against non-citizens voting.

Republican senators say the Supreme Court made the right decision to reject the plan to rework mail-in balloting processes across the United States only a few weeks before Election Day and rebuffed Trump’s angry denunciations of the justices he appointed — including Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

Trump accused Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett, along with Chief Justice John Roberts, of being “bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left” and fumed that the conservative justices he appointed to the court “are merely a shell of their original selves.”

Republican senators recoiled at Trump’s broadside, calling the sharp attacks unwarranted and unfair.

“The president is entitled to his opinion but I don’t agree with him,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), a member of the Judiciary Committee, when asked about Trump’s bullying claim.

“I know every one of the justices. I think they do their very best to call it like they see it and that’s their job,” he said.

Kennedy said the court’s ruling against the last-minute plan to establish new rules for mail-in ballots was not a surprise.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), another member of the Judiciary Committee, said the Trump administration’s effort to mandate a complicated screening process for absentee ballots seven weeks before the election was a recipe for “chaos.”

“It’s too late to implement anyway. It would have been nothing but chaos in the runup to the election,” he said.

“Mail-in ballots are important in many parts of the country because they represent a substantial portion of the overall vote. I don’t know why you would want to restrict mail-in ballots,” he said.

“I’m all for voter integrity measures and there’s plenty of ways to do that but restricting the availability of mail-in ballots is, to me, counterproductive,” he said.

The Trump administration had proposed that states would be required to use special election mail envelopes with unique bar codes that would be scanned by the postal service to guard against the possibility of non-citizens voting.

States would have been required to create lists of voters who are approved to receive mail-in ballots and to upload those lists to a new and little-tested postal service portal.

Kavanaugh, whom Trump appointed to the court in 2018, wrote in a concurring opinion that attempting to rework the mail-in balloting process so close to the election would be “arbitrary and capricious” and would not give state officials enough time to “reasonably implement” changes.

The legal setback enraged Trump who posted on Truth Social: “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.

Cornyn, however, waved off Trump’s declaration that Kavanaugh and other conservative justices had been “bullied” into voting with the Democratic-appointed justices on the court.

“Nah, I don’t believe that. They have lifetime tenure for a reason,” he said, arguing such appointments are designed to insulate justices from political pressure.

“An independent judiciary is really the most important institution in our government,” he said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) also defended the justices who ruled against Trump, noting that the Supreme Court gave Trump a big victory last month by ruling that Trump could continue his controversial White House ballroom construction project.

“The judiciary is trying to be the objective referee on a lot of these issues and a lot of times folks out there disagree with the calls. There are some I disagree with, too. But I just think they’ve got a job to do and they’re an independent branch of the government,” he said.

“We worked hard to get some of those folks confirmed and their job is to be independent and do their best to ensure that they’re interpreting and applying the Constitution and the law in a fair and evenhanded manner,” Thune added.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the Senate Republican Policy Committee chair, argued it’s too late in the election year to require states to create and distribute new ballot envelopes with unique bar codes.

“It’s so close to the election. I don’t know how you implement something like that anyway. I think we’ve got to go with the system we got and let the states run them well just like we do in West Virginia,” she said.

Asked about the president’s criticism of Kavanaugh, Gorsuch and Coney Barret, Capito waved her hand and said, “He can say what he wants.”

Trump’s sharp criticisms of the Federal Reserve Wednesday are also making some Republicans uncomfortable. Trump criticized the central bank after it raised interest rates.

Trump declared that “interest rates in the United States should be 1 percent or less because we are the Best Credit in the World.”

He called on the central bank to “lower the interest rates … and fast!”

Trump later told reporters that he’s “relying” on Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, to cut rates, but gave him the greenlight to “vote with the board” since they had majority support for raising interest rates to between 3.75 percent and 4 percent.

The president lambasted the other board members as “very hostile” and “very political.”

But Republican senators said the Fed members only followed their mandate to keep inflation in check.

“I have no problem with the Fed decision. I think the Fed exercised their independence, which is what we elect them to do, and I think the markets have responded accordingly,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said, calling the financial markets “a true barometer of what’s going on.”

Stocks Fell immediately after the Fed announced the rate hike but then surged on Thursday, with the S&P 500 and the NASDAQ rising 1.14 percent and 1.69 percent, respectively.

“That’s going to help the president long-term. It may not be what he wants short-term but to have a Fed in which the markets has confidence in their ability to look at the economy as a whole, that’s a very important thing for the president to have on his side long-term,” he said. “The Fed did what they were supposed to do.”

“They’re trying their best to ensure that they’re meeting their mission of keeping inflation at the rate that’s called for in their charter,” he said. “It’s always a bit of a judgment call but that’s the conclusion they came to.”

Through Thune acknowledged the rate hike “is not going to be helpful in terms of lowering costs in the near term.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said “the Fed made the right decision yesterday to unanimously raise rates.”

“I think Chairman Warsh for his leadership and displaying the independence needed to get prices under control for everyday Americans,” he posted on X.

Trump’s demand for the Fed to cut interest rates dramatically to 1 percent drew attacks from Democrats, who called the 1-percent interest rate target absurd.

“Every day that goes by, the president seems more detached from reality,” said Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the ranking member of the Banking Committee. “This economy is in real trouble and the idea of a 1 percent interest rate is born of a form of wishful thinking.”

She said that cutting rates down to just 1 percent when inflation is still well above the Fed’s 2 percent target would be a “disaster for our economy.”

articles.title: Impeach Trump, but limit future presidents too
articles.summary: Professor Richard Davis argues that a Democratic majority in Congress should seek to impeach President Trump and implement constitutional reforms to curtail executive powers regarding pardons, war-making and tariffs.
articles.body:
Both the polls and the prediction markets suggest that in the upcoming midterm elections, Democrats will regain the majority in the House of Representatives if not in the Senate as well.

At that point, Democrats will face the question of whether to impeach President Trump once again. Not only should Trump be impeached to hold him accountable for his abuses of power, but Congress also must curb presidential power before another president follows Trump’s lead.

No president has ignored the rule of law as much as Trump. His administration has disregarded court orders , closed departments without congressional approval , engaged in aggressive and illegal immigration enforcement tactics, withheld funds legally authorized by Congress, imposed tariffs unlawfully , and, most recently, waged a war without congressional consent or even notification. No president in our history deserves impeachment and removal from office more than Trump.

Admittedly, even if impeached, Trump will not be removed from office. Even though some Senate Republicans will support removal in a Senate trial, as happened in the past, the likelihood that the two-thirds majority will be achieved is slim. Nevertheless, both the House and the Senate should send the message that presidents cannot act as Trump has without consequences.

But the Congress needs to go further. Powers granted to the executive need to be curtailed to avoid a repetition of the Trump presidency and the potential permanency of the expansion of presidential powers. Congress can do this in several ways.

One immediate need is to pass a constitutional amendment limiting the pardon power. The Framers of the Constitution could not have imagined a president would so abuse the pardon power as Trump has done. Trump has issued more pardons than any president since Harry Truman, although given his current pace of pardoning it is likely he will pass Truman’s record. It is not just the number, but who gets them.

Not only did Trump pardon hundreds of people who rioted on Jan. 6, but he has helped his political allies with pardons as well as those who donate large amounts of money to his causes. Limits need to be placed on self-pardons, pardons of relatives, and individuals who have committed certain crimes. Pardons should be relatively rare and not be part of a quid pro quo that benefits the president. And, definitely, no president should be able to pardon himself, an idea Trump has publicly toyed with .

Another is to limit the president’s war-making power. Congress did this once with the War Powers Act of 1974. Presidents Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon had waged war without congressional approval. The War Powers Act requires congressional consultation and approval. President Trump has ignored those provisions. Congress needs to put more teeth in the War Powers Act, such as an automatic cut-off of war-related funds without a vote of congressional approval.

Trump is claiming the War Powers Act restricts his ability to pursue his war aims against Iran. But that is exactly what it is designed to do. The nation should not go to war on the basis of one individual’s judgment. In a democratic society, such a crucial decision should be made by the people’s representatives, not the executive alone.

Yet another move is to rein in presidential tariff power. Constitutionally, the imposition of tariffs on goods from other countries is the responsibility of Congress. But Congress has granted presidents the power to impose tariffs under certain conditions. Trump has exploited those conditions illegally. Congress needs to impose more limits on those conditions, such as a requirement of congressional approval before a tariff can be imposed or a more explicit description of a real emergency when Congress could be bypassed.

These are just a few of the ways Congress could begin to reassert its Constitutional powers vis-à-vis the president. In the midst of the abuses of the Trump administration, now is a perfect time to take action. Unless such balancing is restored, future presidents will expand presidential power to the extent that Constitutional checks will become meaningless, and presidents will become virtual dictaertors.

Richard Davis is a professor emeritus of political science at BYU. He is the author of several books on American politics.

articles.title: Trump floats nuclear option in Kennedy Center fight
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump hints at demolishing Kennedy Center ▪ Florida GOP congresswoman breaks with Trump ▪ ICE director nomination pulled ▪ Carney open to Canada joining EU President Trump is digging in on the battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center, raising the possibility that his administration could have the institution…
articles.body:
▪ Trump hints at demolishing Kennedy Center

▪ Florida GOP congresswoman breaks with Trump

President Trump is digging in on the battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center, raising the possibility that his administration could have the institution torn down entirely if he doesn’t get his way.

The president was seen on Air Force One on Wednesday night looking at a placard that appears to show the potential demolition of the center. He suggested during a campaign stop in North Carolina that day that his administration could demolish the center if it doesn’t honor Trump in addition to former President John F. Kennedy , and close for renovations of his design.

“So, for the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close,” he told reporters. “It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.”

The increasingly dire warnings from the president follow the latest vote from the center’s board Tuesday to close the main building for renovations. Officials said the center faces “certain fiscal collapse” within weeks and that only an effort to recognize Trump’s contributions to the center would allow him to raise enough money to save it.

The board’s plan to rename the center has now been blocked twice by a federal judge. It was first barred from adding Trump’s name alongside Kennedy’s and more recently prevented from carrying out its alternative plan to inscribe Trump’s name on the building and rename the campus for him.

The Trump-picked board has maintained that the center is unsafe for public occupancy, pointing to a water leak that caused a section of the grand foyer ceiling to fall to the floor. Trump said the closure would take place “immediately,” but the work couldn’t be done until the appeals court for the D.C. Circuit rules on the center’s name change.

The move spurred Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the board, to request an emergency hearing for a federal judge to review the closure vote. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper declined Beatty’s request on Thursday, though he required the federal government to provide at least 30 days’ notice if it intends to demolish the performing arts center.

Cooper previously blocked the board’s earlier attempt to close the center.

The center’s executive director, Matt Floca , said in a court filing Thursday that the main building’s current closure is unrelated to the board’s pursuit of long-term renovations. He said the main building will be closed for at least a week for emergency repairs, noting the water leak and partial ceiling collapse.

Floca said the period could be extended beyond a week if he determines it necessary and the timeline would be evaluated on a weekly basis.

Cooper’s earlier ruling had prohibited the center from being closed for the long term, but he didn’t bar officials from conducting necessary repairs.

“No part of the Court’s preliminary injunction order forbids a temporary closure like this one,” Department of Justice lawyer Brantley Mayers argued.

Meanwhile, the plaintiffs seeking to block the board’s actions are stepping up their response. Eight historical, architectural and preservationist organizations who are plaintiffs against the Kennedy Center on Thursday called for its leaders to either resign or appoint a receiver to oversee the institution.

“The irrevocable loss of this iconic building — whether by intent, neglect or mismanagement — appears increasingly possible,” they said in a statement.

Attorney Greg Werkheiser , whose law firm is one of three representing the plaintiffs, said they will “likely soon” file for a receivership.

He said the institution filing for bankruptcy isn’t necessary for the court to force a change in management. He noted that Congress has set aside $257 million for repairs to the center and argued that Trump has the “extraordinary responsibility” to use his power to keep the center running, not “extraordinary leverage to demand” that it honor him.

If Trump did go through with knocking down part of the center, it wouldn’t be entirely without precedent in his second term. He had the East Wing of the White House torn down unilaterally last year, beginning what’s been another long-running controversy over the construction of a massive ballroom.

▪ The Washington Post : What’s next for the center now that it’s closed?

▪ USA Today : Beatty says Trump ‘threw a tantrum’ during center meeting.

South Florida suddenly came into focus when Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) released a new ad, standing in front of the White House, criticizing President Trump’s immigration policies. She won her race in 2024 by 20 points, leading to questions about that seat now potentially coming into play for Democrats.

I asked Sean Spicer about the ad, and he blasted how Salazar went about her messaging.

“Whoever her consultant cadre that came up with this should never work in Republican politics again. This is the epitome of stupidity,” Spicer said. “There’s no problem putting some daylight between you and the White House. The manner in which she did it, I’m literally appalled at how childish it was.”

We are likely to see more Republican candidates between now and the midterms create that daylight from the White House on issues that play differently back at home. How they go about doing it as well will be another fascinating dynamic to watch.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

A new The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey found Democrat Adam Hamilton narrowly leading Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) by 2 points, within the margin of error. The race is considered a longshot for Democrats, but Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, has given them hope of pulling off an upset.

A man who sprayed vinegar at Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) in January was sentenced to 14 months in prison Thursday as part of a plea deal with prosecutors. He will also undergo three years of supervised release after getting out of prison and was issued a no-contact order with Omar.

The state of Alabama carried out the execution of Jeffery Lee by lethal injection Thursday evening, months after the Supreme Court blocked his execution by nitrogen gas. The case itself was particularly controversial as a judge had overturned a majority vote by the jury for life in prison rather than death, a practice that the state has since eliminated.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) speaks at a 2022 Republican campaign rally in West Miami, Fla., Oct. 19, 2022. (Rebecca Blackwell, Associated Press file)

BIG BREAK: Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) released a television ad Thursday that directly attacked Trump and his hardline immigration tactics.

The move marked a stunning break from the president within his own party and reflected concerns about whether Hispanic voters will turn out for the GOP at the same rate they did for the president in 2024.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said, looking into the camera as she addressed Trump directly.

The president has emphasized that the immigration crackdown is focused on criminals, but the congresswoman noted in the ad that, in July, half of the 50,000 people detained had no criminal record, adding, “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policies.”

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” she said in the 30-second ad spot.

“I’m not talking about giving them amnesty,” Salazar said at the conclusion of the ad. “ I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land, and only you can do that .”

The message is especially notable since Salazar, first elected in 2020, won reelection in her district by 20 points in 2024, and Trump won by more than 14 points. But the Democratic House Majority PAC circulated internal partisan polling showing the race as a toss-up.

▪ The Hill : John Cornyn won’t vote for Bo French in Texas race.

▪ The Hill : Mike Rogers calls for suspension of federal, Michigan gas taxes.

BACKING DOWN : The White House withdrew the nomination of Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to be director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday after it stalled in the Senate.

Trump tapped Schroyer in June, calling him “a PATRIOT with real operational experience.” The selection was supported by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin , a former Oklahoma senator, but surprised some because of his lack of experience leading a major law enforcement agency. Schroyer had once led Mullin’s security detail, and the secretary made Schroyer a senior adviser at DHS shortly after he was confirmed earlier this year.

Senate Homeland Security Committee Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.), who frequently finds himself at odds with Mullin, had yet to schedule a hearing for the nominee, requesting information from DHS on its investigation into two agents accused of killing two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.

A spokesperson for Paul told The Hill that the committee chair “has not expressed opposition to the nominee.”

▪ The Hill : ICE officer arrested in Minnesota on assault charges.

▪ Fox News : Majority say immigration enforcement has crossed a line.

CLIMATE FIGHT : A half dozen environmental and public health organizations sued the Trump administration Thursday over its plan to eliminate most climate regulations on coal and gas power plants.

The administration finalized its move on Monday to gut regulations limiting planet-warming emissions from the plants in what would be a major win for the fossil fuel industry. Under the change, existing coal and new gas plants will no longer have to prevent 90 percent of carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

The administration estimated that it would save about $310 billion. If upheld, the move could be one of the Trump administration’s most consequential climate rollbacks, The Hill’s Rachel Frazin reports.

The groups that sued argued in their complaint that the Environmental Protection Agency has a legal responsibility to limit planet-warming emissions and that not doing so would result in significant health effects.

▪ The Hill : Administration reduces protections for endangered species again.

‘ JON BELONGED TO ALL OF ARIZONA’ : Former Sen. Jon Kyl (R-Ariz.), who served in Congress for more than 25 years, has died from complications from a neurological disease, his family announced . He was 84.

“We know that Jon belonged to all of Arizona, a state he loved and explored with vigor, curiosity, and wonder. Serving his state and nation in Congress was a privilege and responsibility he honored and respected. We are grateful for his full and meaningful public life,” a statement from his family read.

The late senator was diagnosed with dementia late last year and said he would be withdrawing from public life at that time.

Kyl served in the House from 1987 to 1995 and in the Senate from 1995 to 2013, eventually rising to minority whip in the party. He was also appointed to serve for a few months of the late Sen. John McCain ’s (R-Ariz.) term after he died in office in 2018.

▪ KJZZ : Jeff Flake on Kyl: ‘No more committed public servant for Arizona.’

▪ Merced Sun-Star : What to know about the late senator.

The president will greet the Million Dollar Pitch Competition finalists at 1:30 p.m. He will make an announcement on healthcare at 2:30 p.m. and participate in a photo opportunity at 4 p.m. He will participate in signing time at 4:30 p.m. He will travel to Sterling, Va., for a MAGA, Inc., meeting at 6:30 p.m. and dinner at 7:15 p.m. He will then depart for Camp David, where he will spend the weekend.

The Senate will meet at 9 a.m. for a pro forma session

An advertisement for the cryptocurrency Bitcoin is displayed on a building in Hong Kong on Nov. 18, 2021. (Kin Cheung, Associated Press file)

SHIFTING FOCUS : With the push for a sweeping cryptocurrency regulation bill collapsing in the Senate this week, the industry is now turning its attention to federal regulators to set rules.

Every Senate Democrat and several Republicans voted to block a procedural vote Tuesday to advance the Clarity Act, which would set up a regulatory framework for the crypto market. Up to a dozen Democrats were considered potential yes votes, but negotiations fell apart after the two sides failed to reach an agreement on ethics rules amid concerns about the Trump family’s involvement in crypto.

The Hill’s Julia Shapero reports crypto leaders are quickly shifting their hopes to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for oversight.

“The Senate has voted and we have a different type of clarity. It’s time for agencies to step forward and for crypto voters to make their voice heard,” Faryar Shirzad , Coinbase’s chief policy officer, wrote in a post Tuesday on the social platform X.

Patrick Witt , the president’s chief crypto adviser, pointed to the two agencies’ chairs on Tuesday after the bill failed, saying “you’re up.”

The agencies had always been expected to oversee the crypto market, Shapero notes, as the Clarity Act mostly sought to create a framework for splitting responsibilities between them, determining when digital assets are securities or commodities.

The industry preferred more permanent regulations in the form of legislation, but the agencies have already been moving on their own regulations.

CFTC Chair Michael Selig said the agency would “get the job done” using existing statutory authority, while SEC Chair Paul Atkins hinted at upcoming action from the agency. On Thursday, the SEC unveiled its long-awaited “innovation exemption,” which exempts platforms and liquidity providers from traditional securities rules, clearing the way for tokenized stock trading.

▪ The Hill : Senate Democrat blocks bill on data center electricity costs.

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers a speech during a formal sitting at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, eastern France, Sept 17, 2026. (Pascal Bastien, Associated Press)

CANADA EMBRACES EU: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney embraced the idea of joining the European Union as its first associate member, a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen publicly floated the idea as a way to strengthen their alliance.

“A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies,” Carney said in remarks before the European Parliament. “An alliance not defined by what we oppose but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability.”

“Canada welcomes this ambition,” he added, pointing to polling that shows strong support among Canadians for “much closer ties with Europe.”

A day earlier, the European commissioner addressed Carney directly in a social media post, saying, “Dear @MarkJCarney we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the EU,” she added. “And create a common prosperity and economic security space.”

The suggestion of an associate membership for Canada comes amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and its neighbor to the north. The Trump administration levied high tariffs on Canadian goods in recent weeks as trade talks fizzled , and he threatened to levy additional economic consequences if Canada joins the EU.

“I think it’s laughable. Canada’s been a terrible trading partner,” Trump said about the proposal.

“If they do that, if I think at all it’s a hostile act,” he added. “I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe.”

▪ WMUR : Canada’s EU membership could increase U.S. costs.

President Trump is bringing healthy food from harvest to hallways , Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. write in The Hill.

Trust in America’s food safety system is crumbling — Congress can restore it , Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-Md.) writes in The Hill.

Former first lady Barbara Bush, her granddaughter Barbara, and Millie wait on the steps of the White House for Former President George H.W. Bush to return from his 1991 check-up at Bethesda Naval Hospital in Washington. (Barry Thumma, Associated Press file)

Here’s who went 4/4: Richard Baznik, Stan Wasser, Chuck Schoenenberger, Carmine Petracca, Michael Salanik, Linda L. Field, Harry Strulovici, Rick Schmidtke, Marcia Gatlin, Jenessa Wagner, Mark R. Williamson, Ned Sauthoff, M. Whitehouse, David Newton, Jim Anderson, Robert Bradley and Steve James .

Other than Trump, two presidents didn’t have any pets — James Polk and Andrew Johnson. While Johnson didn’t have any official pets, he was said to have taken care of some mice that lived in the White House.

Theodore Roosevelt had the most pets of any commander-in-chief , owning 11 horses, six dogs, five guinea pigs, two cats and various other animals, including a bear, a pig, a badger and a hen.

Barbara Bush wrote a children’s book from the point of view of her family’s English spaniel Millie , published in 1990. Millie is the only presidential pet to have a book from her perspective.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: How a little more ‘pearl clutching’ would have helped GOP
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] In the run-up to last fall’s state elections in…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

In the run-up to last fall’s state elections in Virginia and New Jersey, Democrats belatedly found a weapon to use against the barrage of GOP attacks on the blue team’s nominee for Virginia attorney general.

The episode understandably has faded from memory because, as it turned out, it was a meaningless spin cycle. Jay Jones , the candidate who had sent creepy, cruel texts to a Republican former statehouse colleague, won in a breeze. He came in a little more than 4 points behind the top of the ticket, but a big blue wave in both states carried all the Democratic candidates, good and bad, to victory.

For a moment in October, though, when polls suggested some uncertainty in that outcome, Republicans zeroed in on Jones — very progressive, inexperienced and running to be the first Black attorney general in the commonwealth’s history — as a way to frighten law-and-order suburbanites and to suggest the moderation expressed by Democrats was only a ruse to gain power.

Anxious Democrats breasted a great sigh of relief when the story of the Young Republican group chat broke loose. A former member of the group for Republicans under age 40 (young being a relative term) had leaked the messages with all manner of horrible stuff: racism, antisemitism, gay slurs and jokes about gas chambers, slavery and rape. And some of those involved were or had become staffers with official positions in the party.

Democratic spinmeisters had a way to reclaim the narrative about nasty electronic communications. Any question about Jones could be answered with an “Oh, yeah. How about your holocaust jokes?” Most Republicans confronted with the messages were quick to denounce and disavow them and their senders. But into this panic strode Vice President Vance , cool and collected, telling his fellow Republicans not to take the bait.

These “edgy, offensive jokes” told by “kids” — “especially young boys” — who “do stupid things” should not “ruin their lives.” The most important thing , Vance said, was to keep the focus on Jones in Virginia: “I refuse to join the pearl clutching when powerful people call for political violence.”

But, of course, the question of whether to clutch or not to clutch was immaterial. The rout was on. Indeed, insofar as the question of which texts were worse mattered to any persuadable voter, a lack of pearl clutching may actually have hurt Republicans’ performance. If you were one of the many fiscally conservative, socially moderate suburbanites in Virginia or New Jersey concerned about the unsavory elements of the post-Jan. 6 GOP, it might have been comforting to hear party leaders take the chuds behind the rhetorical woodshed.

Vance, though, made it clear that these 30-something-year-olds should be shielded to deny Democrats to deflect from Jones. But that’s not how campaign communications work. Refusing to condemn the Young Republicans leaders didn’t lessen attention to the scandal, but rather increased it. Ask any Democrat this year how well deflect-to-protect has worked with the initial efforts to “move on” from their own chud faction, especially Graham Platner and Hasan Piker . Vance imagined a stone wall, but instead provided a gate through which the story could charge ahead.

We can mostly leave aside how Vance’s personal ambitions may have interfered with the counsel he provided to his party. But it is fair to say that Vance launched his efforts to minimize the offense in an interview with Turning Point USA, the group for campus right-wingers founded by Charlie Kirk . Turning Point USA is a centerpiece of Vance’s 2028 campaign and is an important part of his bid to block any challenger from his right. He was presumably talking more to the very online, young, male podcast audience than any suburban moms in Leesburg, Va., or Parsippany, N.J.

But, again, it probably didn’t matter much to the election results in those states what Vance said. The climate had already turned very cold for the Republicans, and swing voters were swinging hard back to the Democrats after a good year for the GOP in 2024. But that doesn’t mean Vance’s strategy didn’t have political consequences.

Remember that the Jones-Young Republicans imbroglio was before the Iran war, surging prices, steep mortgage rates, the massive personal paydays for President Trump and everything else that has afflicted the red team this year. The climate of a year ago looks positively balmy compared with what the GOP is facing now.

In other words, now is not a good time for Republicans to again be debating the appropriateness of white nationalism , Nazi imagery , deeming oneself a “ heritage American ” and dealing in antisemitic tropes . The recent eruptions of right-wing bigotry are bad, regardless of their political implications. But to compound the problem for Republicans, this flood comes at exactly the moment the GOP is trying to use Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed ’s radicalism on Israel to tar his whole party.

Vance told House Republicans this week to use El-Sayed in any race in which the actual Democrat is “not that crazy.” Not a terrible strategy. Both parties have long profited by enthusiastic use of part-to-whole fallacies . But if you want to say that the other side is full of kooky bigots, it is helpful if you have mopped up your own kooks and bigots first. If Republicans are trying to do with El-Sayed what they tried to do with Jones last year, they would have a much easier time of it if the vice president and others had sent the clear signal in 2025 that they had no tolerance for that kind of bad behavior.

Instead, Republicans, still riding the “vibe shift” of the 2024 election, tried to redefine the rules of the game. “Pearl clutching” and “ endless, self-defeating purity tests ” were out. It was time, we were told, that “you don’t have to apologize for being white anymore.” It is not surprising that many actual bigots heard these things as dog whistles calling them out in the open.

And they have shown up, barking mad, at exactly the moment it would help Republicans for them to be chained up under the porch.

The Atlantic : “Most retrospectives unfold like a stately procession. You buy your ticket and proceed through a choreographed sequence of galleries, scrutinizing first the juvenilia, then the promising early work. Next come the triumphal years, and finally (if the artist was lucky) a poignant late phase. An idea of timelessness prevails, enhanced by an enveloping atmosphere of climate control, security, and massive insurance coverage. The lighting is good; the frames are tasteful. Everything looks marvelous. There’s not a whiff of the urgency of the studio, no hint of the emotional or psychological state in which these objects were made. Lost is any suggestion of that feeling, deep inside the creator, of an improvised, inner necessity. ‘ Willem de Kooning Drawing,’ at the Art Institute of Chicago, is a classic retrospective—a decorous, deeply researched exhibition about a much-lauded artist at a major museum. In another, more robust sense, however, the show is a giant debauch. It’s frankly (and thrillingly) unseemly. I’ve never been to an art show that takes you so far inside the creative process. articles.body:
Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate running for Senate in Kansas, says he will not support Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) serving another term as Democratic leader if the megachurch pastor defeats Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in November.

“I’m not supporting Schumer for leader,” Hamilton told CNN’s Kasie Hunt in an interview. “I’m saying let’s look to see who might we have that would be a leader to unite us and bring us together.”

Hamilton said there is widespread voter dissatisfaction with gridlock and partisanship in Washington and suggested that Schumer, who has been Democratic leader since 2017, is part of the problem.

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer but we need new leadership. We need new younger leadership, young blood. I don’t mean just age but people who are bringing fresh ideas and fresh leadership. In Kansas, Chuck Schumer’s a liability for Democrats,” he said.

“We’ve got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together – not just Democrats – but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems. I think people are frustrated with the gridlock and the sense that people are not working together to solve problems,” he said.

Hamilton pointed to Democrats blocking the farm bill in the Senate Agriculture Committee last month even though Republicans offered a major concession in proposing to delay the implementation of cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by a year.

“As an independent minded Democrat, I’m going to work with Republicans on that and we’re going to get this through,” he said. “I think people are frustrated, we have to do better.”

Hamilton is one of several Senate Democratic candidates who say they won’t support Schumer serving another term or have declined to endorse his continued leadership of the Senate Democratic caucus.

Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic candidate in Minnesota, and Juliana Stratton in Illinois, and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in Michigan, have withheld their support from Schumer serving another two years as leader.

A new The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey showed Hamilton leading Marshall, 45 to 43 percent.

Kansas last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1932.

articles.title: The center-left needs to step up and show America what it stands for
articles.summary: They only need to dust off their own rich legacy of bold and modernizing reform rooted in America’s liberal tradition.
articles.body:
These are tough times for center-left parties, which increasingly find themselves squeezed into a shrinking middle ground by populist insurgents on the right and left. Few are rising to the challenge of offering restive voters an inspiring alternative to populist prescriptions for sweeping economic and political change.

That leaves most of the political passion and energy churning on the political extremes. MAGA and the Democratic Socialists of America certainly don’t lack bold ideas for change. Even if they do more harm than good, like President Trump’s inflationary tariffs, or unravel under scrutiny, like progressive proposals to abolish private health insurance and pay for a wide array of so-called free public goods by taxing wealth.

But even if they’re peddling snake oil, right- and left-wing populists have sharply defined beliefs and earn points for strong convictions. The center-left, in contrast, suffers from an identity crisis: Voters have only a fuzzy idea of what it stands for. Worse, working-class voters here and across Europe tend to lump center-left and center-right parties into an out-of-touch political establishment that ignores their struggles and governs on behalf of affluent elites and entrenched interests.

What should center-left parties like the Democrats offer voters? Moderation? Compromise and bipartisanship? Political civility? There’s something to be said for each of these, but they don’t add up to a compelling governing philosophy.

Nor is this a time for policy incrementalism. Working Americans are fed up with economic arrangements they see as deeply unfair, the fracturing of our national identity and civic unity and a sclerotic federal government’s inability to get big things done. They’re looking for structural remedies for structural problems.

Democrats aren’t condemned to vapid centrism. They only need to dust off their own rich legacy of bold and modernizing reform rooted in America’s liberal tradition.

It includes Woodrow Wilson’s progressive reforms of early 20th century, which enabled the federal government to adapt to a rapidly industrializing and urbanizing America, Roosevelt’s New Deal for “ bold, persistent experimentation ” to combat the Great Depression, Harry Truman’s postwar design of a new architecture for national and collective security, Lyndon Johnson’s forceful advocacy of landmark civil rights laws and Bill Clinton’s “ New Democrat ” innovations for reducing welfare dependence and crime, creating alternatives to failing public schools and reinventing rather than simply expanding government.

The big question today is whether Democrats will replicate this fusion of radically pragmatic means to liberal ends or keep moving left. Pressure to do just that accelerated dramatically this past summer as young democratic socialists successfully challenged liberal and even progressive Democratic incumbents in primary campaigns.

The populist left complains that mainstream Democrats aren’t fighting hard enough against President Trump. That’s ironic, since their ideas have made a major contribution to Democrats’ present minority status by alienating working-class voters. When you’re completely out of power, you don’t have many weapons to fight with.

Yet some party leaders hope to co-opt leftist energy even while distancing themselves from ideas that excite white college liberals but leave swing voters cold.

U.S. liberals historically have found common ground with European social democrats, like Britain’s Labour Party. Both support a mixed economy that combines free markets and private enterprise with government intervention and public services. But U.S. liberalism and socialist-style anti-capitalism, collectivism and cultural radicalism are fundamentally incompatible creeds . Mushing them together will only compound the center-left’s hazy profile.

It’s not enough for Democrats to oppose left-wing ideas as electoral losers. They also need to say why those ideas are wrong on the merits. Otherwise, they’ll leave the impression of a weak center-left that won’t fight for its own principles.

For example, Democrats should unequivocally reject progressive demands to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a de facto return to open borders, which violates Americans’ right to decide who enters our country and on what terms. The same goes for progressive demands for Medicare for All, which carries an astronomical price tag of at least $35 trillion over a decade.

The center-left should also steer clear of slopulist proposals that promise everyone new tax cuts or new government benefits supposedly paid for by soaking the rich. Instead, Democrats should target tax relief on working families, by cutting payroll taxes and replacing the lost revenue with a progressive consumption tax.

Nor should the center-left let anti-AI populists define the party’s position on this supremely important issue. Rather than joining the progressive stampede to block data centers, Democrats should focus on erecting a public safety framework that mandates human control over self-improving AI. The risks of a break-out are large; so are the potential rewards of turbo-charging economic productivity and scientific endeavors with AI.

By defining itself clearly as a liberal force for fundamental reform in politics and government, the center-left can help move America past today’s polarizing populism.

Will Marshall is president and founder of Progressive Policy Institute.
